The actions of the pilot of Aircraft Y clearly rose to the level of 14 CFR 91.13 'careless and reckless.',,,,SR-22 Instructor reported executing a successful evasive maneuver during initial climb due to an NMAC event with another aircraft landing on the opposite runway.
1758846,202008,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,10000,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Travelair 95,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,None,Class C ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Propeller Control,,X,Improperly Operated,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Facility X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Air Transport Pilot (ATP); Flight Crew Flight Engineer; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 125.9; Flight Crew Total 22537; Flight Crew Type 29.3,,Troubleshooting; Confusion; Situational Awareness,,,1758846,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,On a multiengine training flight the Commercial ASEL rated student pilot was at the controls of the aircraft. With the 'pre-landing' and 'landing checklist' complete; we had been cleared to land on [Runway] XX at ZZZ. Descending through 500 AGL as part of my 'stabilized approach' check; I visually confirmed GUMPS complete with the mixture levers 'Rich' and the prop levers full forward 'High RPM'. During the normal round out / flare for landing on XX; the aircraft suddenly dropped and landed very hard and bounced back into the air approximately 10 to 15 feet AGL. I took control of the aircraft at this time and applied full throttle and rotated slightly to a Go Around attitude. The engines while running did not develop max thrust and the airplane did not accelerate normally. The aircraft drifted left of the runway; yawed to the left; rolled left and started to settle back to ground. As the roll to the left continued; I became concerned about flight at speeds below Vmc speed and departure of controlled flight. So I closed both throttles as I continued to apply right rudder pressure to align the aircraft with the direction of travel. As the aircraft drifted left and settled with the nose starting to rotate back to the right; I believe the left-wing tip touched the ground and helped to level the aircraft as the aircraft touched down slightly nose low and yawed slightly right of the direction of travel. The aircraft came to a stop. I was uninjured and asked the Commercial ASEL rated student pilot if she was ok and she replied yes. Our headsets and glasses had been thrown off during the landing. I put my headset back on as ZZZ's tower was calling our N number. I told them that we were alright but to please roll the airport CFR equipment and that I'd be securing the aircraft.While securing the aircraft ... fuel shut off valves - closed; mixture levers - idle cutoff; throttles - closed. It was then that I noticed that the propeller levers were in the 'Feather' detent instead of full forward in the 'low pitch' or high RPM position. Then it occurred to me that the rated student pilot had pulled the prop levers to the 'Feather' position instead of closing the throttles as the aircraft settled the last 5 to 10 feet for landing. This explained why the aircraft slammed down to a hard landing and bounced back into the air on what seemed to be a very normal round out / flare to landing. It also explains why the engines; while running - did not develop the required thrust and normal aircraft acceleration with full power applied. I continued with the rest of the shut-down. Avionics master - off; Generators - off; Magnetos L & R engines - off; battery switch off.'Human Performance Considerations'Reflecting on the round out / flare portion of the flight. My attention and focus were outside of the aircraft and down the runway. Concentrating on height; drift and runway alignment as appropriate. I didn't perceive the rated Commercial ASEL student pilot moving the prop levers to feather as opposed to reducing power to facilitate the landing. With the immediate reduction in thrust from the propellers as they started to move towards feather; the aircraft slammed down and bounced. I guard the throttle quadrant (hand below but near the throttles in the event of a go around). But I would not have perceived wrong lever movement. I was quick to respond to the bad bounce with full throttle on both engines but my attention was outside the aircraft in an attempt to control the aircraft. An additional human factor consideration. The Commercial ASEL rated student had previously flown a Cessna 172RG. The throttle/ prop arrangement working left to right is throttle/ propeller/ mixture. In the BE95 the power lever arrangement is propeller/ throttle/ mixture. This was only the second time the Commercial ASEL rate student pilot operated the BE95 type.,,,,Instructor Pilot reported loss of control during landing;  by the student; due to improper landing procedure.
1759568,202009,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,,5400,,,Fog; Haze / Smoke; 10,,Daylight,7000,,TRACON ZZZ,FBO,Skylane 182/RG Turbo Skylane/RG,,1,Part 91,IFR,Training,GPS,Descent; Cruise,Vectors,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,TRACON ZZZ,,Small Aircraft,,,,IFR,,,Initial Approach,Vectors,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Student; Flight Crew Private,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 23; Flight Crew Total 321; Flight Crew Type 14,,Communication Breakdown; Confusion,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1759568,Facility ZZZ.TRACON,,Government,Approach,Air Traffic Control Fully Certified,Air Traffic Control Time Certified In Pos 1 (yrs) 1,,Communication Breakdown; Workload,Party1 ATC; Party2 Flight Crew,,1759576,ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT,,,Automation Air Traffic Control; Person Air Traffic Control,In-flight,Air Traffic Control Issued Advisory / Alert; Flight Crew Became Reoriented; Flight Crew FLC complied w / Automation / Advisory,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was on an IFR training flight in Aircraft X. I was on vectors to ZZZZZ1 over ZZZZZ2 at 6;000 ft. with Approach; expecting the RNAV XX approach at ZZZ. At a few miles from ZZZZZ2; Approach gave me the instruction; 'Aircraft X descend and maintain 4;500 ft. direct ZZZZZ.' I read back; 'Descending 4;500 ft. direct ZZZZZ Aircraft X.' NorCal didn't give a response to my readback; so I proceeded to comply with the instruction. A few moments later; NorCal gave me an altitude advisory saying I was below MVA and was told to immediately climb to 6;000 ft.,,I had 3 aircraft setting up for the GPS XX approach at ZZZ. #1 was Aircraft Y who was 5 miles south-southeast of ZZZZZ; IAF for ZZZ. #2 was Aircraft Z who was about 20 miles south of ZZZZZ; and #3 was Aircraft X who was about 20 east of ZZZZZ. Aircraft X checked on to my frequency level at 6000 on a heading. I acknowledged Aircraft X; told the aircraft to fly heading 200 and maintain 6000; he would be #3. After a few other transmissions; I cleared Aircraft Y to maintain 4500 until established on the approach and cleared GPS XX approach ZZZ. Aircraft X read back; 'Roger maintain 4500 till established;' which I missed.I then vectored a VFR aircraft away from a TFR. Then; Aircraft Y said; 'We copied; maintain 4500 till established; cleared approach.' After a few more transmissions I recognized that Aircraft X was descending below the assigned altitude of 6000. At 5600 which was the MVA in the area; I questioned Aircraft X why he was descending and to maintain 6000; with no response. As Aircraft X was descending below 5400 and now in the MVA; I issued a low altitude alert for Aircraft X and instructed him to climb and maintain 6000 immediately; which he acknowledged and complied. After asking Aircraft X what had happened; he responded that his auto pilot had shut off; and he was apologetic. I missed the hearback/readback. However; I never would have thought that the aircraft that was on a heading 20 miles away from the IAF would take a clearance to maintain 4500 till established and cleared approach. The pilot was issued a brasher; and upon further review I missed Aircraft X taking a clearance for Aircraft Y. Be vigilant listening to call signs and instructions on hearback/readbacks.,,C182 Student Pilot and ATC Controller reported the former taking the clearance of another aircraft and descended below the MVA as a result.
1760212,202009,1201-1800,AJO.Airport,CA,,,300,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,CTAF AJO,FBO,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 2 Eng; Retractable Gear,,1,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Final Approach,,Class G ZLA,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Cessna Aircraft Undifferentiated or Other Model,,1,Part 91,None,,,Final Approach,,Class G ZLA,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 76; Flight Crew Total 1019; Flight Crew Type 268,,Communication Breakdown; Workload,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1760212,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 100,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action; Flight Crew Executed Go Around / Missed Approach,Human Factors,Human Factors,My student and I performed the Practice VOR-A approach into AJO. 1760237,202009,,ZZZ.Airport,US,350,5,,6500,,VMC,10,,Daylight,12000,,,FBO,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Cruise,None,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 1; Flight Crew Total 1200; Flight Crew Type 1000,,Distraction; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1760237,,,,,,,,,,,,Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Exited Penetrated Airspace,Environment - Non Weather Related; Human Factors,Human Factors,Performed an intercom check on the ground; between myself and passenger; which was satisfactory. Departed on an introductory training flight as the instructor. It was my second flight using a mask required by our flight school's new COVID-19 related policies and procedures. The route of flight was to be per my normal introductory flight. Turned south towards ZZZ after above a safe altitude. Experienced difficulty communicating with the passenger as my mask was interfering with my microphone. I repositioned my headset's microphone from the outside to the inside of the mask which resolved the communication problem. At this point I identified the road which runs tangentially to the northern edge of the lateral boundary of ZZZ's Class D airspace. After initiating my usual turn to the West to avoid the Class D airspace; I realized that I had mistakenly used the wrong road which was 1 mile south of the correct road and I was now in ZZZ's Class D airspace. I continued turn to a northerly heading in order to exit the airspace and then continued on the introductory flight's route as usual. I was momentarily distracted and failed to maintain situational awareness. As a result; I entered Class D airspace before establishing radio contact. Once the airplane began to turn; the error was apparent and immediately corrected. I should have prioritized tasks and addressed the intercom problem after ensuring correct navigation and situational awareness.,,,,Flight instructor reported difficulty talking to passenger while wearing a face mask and had an airspace violation while attempting to fix the communication issue.
1760260,202009,0601-1200,SET.Airport,MO,,10,1000,,,VMC,20,,Daylight,,,,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Cruise,None,Class E ZKC,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Amateur/Home Built/Experimental,,,Part 91,,,,,,Class E ZKC,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 175; Flight Crew Total 400; Flight Crew Type 330,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1760260,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Airborne Conflict; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 50; Vertical 50,,Automation Aircraft Terrain Warning,,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,While practicing ground reference maneuvers with my pre-solo private pilot student; I noticed a plane flying on a course that would intercept our maneuvering area. My ADSB-in noticed the plane and soon after I had visual contact. I made announcements of my position on the local CTAF that is used in that area; due to the proximity of the airport that the flight training is conducted out of. No response was made by the incoming aircraft. Due to my position I took controls from my student and altered our course to the right in an attempt to clear the area. Aircraft Y flew towards me as indicated by my ADSB equipment; as well as the small amount of visual contact I had as the aircraft moved to a chasing position. Slow controlled turns were made to try to get the aircrafts attention (I did not know if Aircraft Y had me in visual contact) as well as vacate the area due to this aircraft. The collision avoidance sounded multiple times that Aircraft Y was on a direct collision course with me; and indicating on my screen that we had less than 100 ft. of vertical and horizontal clearance. In the closest proximity I was unable to maintain visual contact due to the other aircraft being behind me; and slightly above me. This continued on for a period of somewhere between 3-5 minutes. No matter the direction I flew to try and vacate the area Aircraft Y stayed on my tail. All attempts to establish radio contact failed. The traffic eventually vacated the area to the south of our position.Looking back I should have called St. Louis Approach and let them know of the situation; giving them the opportunity to try to establish radio contact and let the pilot of Aircraft Y know we were a training flight that was not comfortable flying in formation as well as let ATC know that this aircraft was breaking the law and creating a dangerous situation for themselves as well as others.,,,,C172 pilot reported an NMAC with another light aircraft.

I departed the pattern to the south and climbed to 2000 ft. My headset went quiet and I performed a radio check to traffic with no response. I decided there may be a problem with my new headset. At the same time I noticed the airplane temperature was getting hotter and I was concerned about the temperature. I pulled the power back to bring the temperature back down. I attempted to call my instructor but realized he would not be able to hear me. I turned back toward ZZZ but I had lost situational awareness due to the fact that the smoke from the fires had intensified. I headed toward a familiar road and landmark and traversed back and forth above the landmark. I found my bearings by using Foreflight. I texted my instructor and told him the situation and he provided a heading to help me get my bearings as well. I landed the airplane at ZZZ. When I landed my instructor informed me that I had inadvertently flown into [class] C airspace.,,,,C172 student pilot reported inadvertently violating Class C airspace.
1761062,202009,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,,,,,,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Initial Climb,,Class C ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ZZZ,,Small Aircraft,,1,,,,,Initial Climb,,Class C ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument,,,Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Workload; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1761062,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Airborne Conflict; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types,Horizontal 0; Vertical 100,,Automation Aircraft TA,In-flight,Air Traffic Control Issued New Clearance; Air Traffic Control Separated Traffic; Air Traffic Control Provided Assistance; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,Flight crew for this flight; which was my student and I; were flying traffic normally without missing radio call; looking for traffic the entire time. 1761576,202009,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,,,CTAF ZZZ,FBO,Beechcraft Twin Piston Undifferentiated or Other Model,,1,Part 91,None,Skydiving,,Landing,Visual Approach,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying; Captain; Single Pilot,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Air Transport Pilot (ATP); Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 169; Flight Crew Total 1683; Flight Crew Type 151,,Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure,,,1761576,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Gear Up Landing,,,,,,Human Factors,Human Factors,[In] my preflight noticed that both engines needed a quart of oil. Filled both back to the proper indication. Closed both engines then continued with my preflight. Found nothing else that needed attention. I took my first load. I noticed a slightly low oil pressure on that flight and called another King Air pilot that trained me to ask about it. As I got out of the plane the owner and I noticed that oil was all over the left wing. Opened it up and I did not properly secure the oil stick/cap. A small amount of oil was still visible on the stick. I called the A and P and we were advised to put oil back in the engine; clean it up out of the bay and try a run up. The start went normally; oil pressure was back. I taxied down to the end of XX did another run up. Everything was in the normal range. Did a normal takeoff left hand pattern while watching the left engine. Proceeded to a normal approach rounded out; pulled power back then heard the gear unsafe warning. A split second later heard tick of a prop hitting the ground. My initial reaction was to push the power forward and take off but reason took over and I pulled power all the way back and bellied the plane in. Then I secured the plane and got out.I did several things wrong that day most importantly I did not follow the checklist and I did not do a GUMPS (Gas; Undercarriage; Mixture; Prop; Switches) check. I also had been driving 4 hours prior to the event. I am devastated. I should have followed the checklist.,,,,Pilot reported a gear up landing.
1761704,202009,1201-1800,ZZZ.TRACON,US,,,,4000,,Mixed,10,,Daylight,6000,,TRACON ZZZ,FBO,PA-28 Cherokee/Archer/Dakota/Pillan/Warrior,,2,Part 91,IFR,Training,,Cruise,,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Other PART 141 FLIGHT SCHOOL,PA-28 Cherokee/Archer/Dakota/Pillan/Warrior,,,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Other MANUEVERING,None,Class E Y,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Total 817,,Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1761704,,,,,,,,,,,,Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance,Horizontal 100; Vertical 500,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,General None Reported / Taken,Airspace Structure; Company Policy; Human Factors,Human Factors,Aircraft X was operating on an IFR flight plan; and was transitioning through the practice area. During the transition; we received no less than 3 altitude alerts from ATC about company traffic. However; we were in and out of the clouds; IMC. Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z were both observed passing 500 ft. above our aircraft. While observing these two aircraft; they came within 500 ft. both horizontally and vertically of clouds while they were operating VFR. This included Aircraft Y endangering our aircraft by flying within 1;000 ft. of us while we were IMC; presumably bringing them well within the VFR cloud clearance requirements. 1761737,202009,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,,,,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,1,Part 91,None,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Company,,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 75; Flight Crew Total 900; Flight Crew Type 850,,Communication Breakdown; Training / Qualification,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Maintenance,,1761737,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,,,Person Maintenance,Routine Inspection,General Maintenance Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,Apparently one of the flight school aircraft; a Cessna 172-L model; has been technically un-airworthy. The local mechanic shop did perform a pre-buy inspection when the flight school purchased the aircraft. The aircraft has undergone routine 100 hour inspections since the plane started working in the flight school. However; it wasn't until the most recent 100 hour inspection which was early September of this year that the local mechanic shop found that the aircraft was overdue on an Airworthiness Directive on a component on the propeller. It was overdue for about 500 hours on that particular AD. The mechanic shop was not certified to do the inspection on the propeller for that given AD for the propeller to be complied with. The flight school requested a ferry permit to fly the aircraft to the nearest propeller mechanic shop but was denied by the local FSDO. The next option was to remove the propeller and drive it to a propeller shop so that AD could be complied with. Such action was taken and the propeller shop found no defects with the propeller. The propeller was later driven back to the home airport to be placed back on the aircraft. Alas; the aircraft was complied with all known Airworthiness directives. The local mechanic shop staff admitted that they overlooked the AD. However; at the end of the day it is the owner/operator of the aircraft that is ultimately responsible for determining the airworthiness of the aircraft; which includes me; the flight instructor when using the aircraft to train student pilots. The flight school staff; meaning all the instructors and chief pilot were essentially responsible for this oversight of the airworthiness of the aircraft. I believe that the flight school staff trusted the mechanic shop to ensure the aircraft complies with all known AD's for every 100 hour inspection. The flight school has every intention to ensure the aircraft meets all inspections including ADs; and that by paying the mechanic shop for their services would suffice for ensuring the aircraft is airworthy. Over-relying on the mechanic shop in my opinion has been the root cause of this issue. I've personally shown the logbooks of the aircraft and ADs to my students prior to every checkride to show the aircraft is airworthy. I've even presented the ADs to my examiner for my CFI initial checkride. I honestly just never knew how to look up ADs or even know how to make sure that all ADs are complied with. The resolution that the chief pilot and I want to take to prevent this mishap from happening again is to learn how to look up ADs ourselves as a secondary check on top of the routine inspections done by the mechanics. Had I known that the AD wasn't complied with no one would've flown that aircraft until it is absolutely airworthy. A more thorough overview on the flight school's ADs is needed to make sure we are complying with them; and to make sure none have been overlooked. Again; the Chief pilot and I want to be able to double check AD compliance after routine inspections; and enhance communication between the instructors and mechanics.,,,,Flight Instructor reported that an Airworthiness Directive had been overlooked on a flight school aircraft.
1761740,202009,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,1,,1400,,VMC,10,,Daylight,12000,,CTAF ZZZ,FBO,PA-28 Cherokee/Archer/Dakota/Pillan/Warrior,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Final Approach,,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,UAV - Unpiloted Aerial Vehicle,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 121; Flight Crew Total 519; Flight Crew Type 500,,Situational Awareness; Time Pressure,,,1761740,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 50; Vertical 0,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Environment - Non Weather Related; Human Factors,Human Factors,While practicing landings in the pattern at ZZZ. Myself and my student were downwind at 1400 feet MSL when we noticed a drone flying at the same altitude but heading north directly in our path. We took an evasive maneuver by banking to the right to fly around the drone. The drone did not alter course; heading; or altitude. Had we not maneuvered a head on mid-air collision was inevitable.  After I reported this over the CTAF; Unicom attempted to contact the drone operator via the radio frequency but with no luck. This drone seemed to resemble that of an amateur photography style not a professional.,,,,Instructor Pilot reported a NMAC with a UAV while in the traffic pattern.

1765552,202010,1201-1800,SQL.Tower,CA,120,1,400,,,,7,,,,,Tower SQL,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,Visual Approach,Class D SQL,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower SQL,Personal,Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer,,1,Part 91,None,,,Landing,Visual Approach,Class D SQL,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 183; Flight Crew Total 2371; Flight Crew Type 1511,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness,Party1 ATC; Party2 Flight Crew,,1765552,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Conflict Airborne Conflict,Horizontal 100; Vertical 10,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action; Flight Crew Requested ATC Assistance / Clarification,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was in Aircraft X following Aircraft Y along with Aircraft Z. All three aircraft were doing pattern work for at least 30 minutes prior to the incident. For the most part ATC was requiring full stop taxi backs.My plane; Aircraft X; was cleared to land number 2 after Aircraft Y; which was cleared to land number 1.I watched Aircraft Y turn a 1 mile base over the channel coming from the cement plant; which is the typical position for base to final for traffic at San Carlos; soon after receiving sequence and clearance to land. As Aircraft Y approached its turn to final; I saw Aircraft Z on an extended final on a direct collision course with Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y confirmed sequence #2 as opposed to #1 cleared to land and took evasive action.Aircraft Y performed evasive action; 45-60 degree bank turn climbing; and narrowly missed Aircraft Z. Aircraft Z did not change course or direction. ATC then amended the clearance for Aircraft Y to Number 2 for landing and amended my clearance for number 3 for landing. Both planes Aircraft Y and Z landed safely and parked. Somehow; ATC mixed up the sequence. I suspect most likely both Aircraft Y and Z were cleared to land and it was only that the pilot on Aircraft Y looked up the approach path and saw Aircraft Z; and took evasive action that a midair collision was averted.,,,,Flight Instructor reported a near midair collision in the airport traffic pattern.
1766568,202010,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,,,CTAF ZZZ,FBO,Piper Single Undifferentiated or Other Model,,,Part 91,None,Personal,,Landing,None,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Single Pilot,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 74; Flight Crew Total 425; Flight Crew Type 4,,Training / Qualification,,,1766568,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,,Weather; Human Factors,Human Factors,As part of my job as a CFI for a local flight school; I was looking to add tailwheel instruction to my list of instruction services I provide. I have about 15 total tailwheel hours; but very little recent experience. In order to improve proficiency; I went up with an instructor the day before the ground loop to get tailwheel current and get some additional training. We flew for an hour and did four full stop landings on the airfield's grass runway; and all were straight; and no issues came up during any of these landings that would suggest I needed additional training. On the day of the ground loop; the winds had shifted to be about 8 knots directly down the asphalt runway so I chose to use that one rather than the grass which would have had a 90-degree crosswind. During my first approach; I made a low pass to verify the sight picture in my mind and double check any wind correction that may need to be done. I executed a go around and came around for another uneventful approach to a planned 3-point landing. After a smooth touchdown with the airplane rolling down the runway; a gust lifted the right wing and a yaw to the left. My corrective actions did not prevent the airplane from ground looping. Upon reflection; there was a moment where I should have applied power to try to stop the yaw and execute a go-around. However; I believe my ego got in the way since I've been flying more than I ever have that I could 'save' the landing despite teaching my students to default to a go-around when things aren't looking right. My overconfidence in my skills; combined with ego resulted in me trying to save the rollout rather than going around. I also believe more than an hour of recurrent training prior to flying a tailwheel airplane is required; even though I have been flying a lot lately.,,,,Flight Instructor flying a PA-16 aircraft reports ground loop on landing rollout.
1766728,202010,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,12,,,,,,Daylight,,,UNICOM ZZZ,FBO,DA20 Undifferentiated,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Takeoff / Launch,,Class G ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 45; Flight Crew Total 274; Flight Crew Type 13.5,,Time Pressure; Other / Unknown; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1766728,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Object; Ground Excursion Runway,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Regained Aircraft Control; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action; General Flight Cancelled / Delayed; General Maintenance Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,Loss of control during student simulated soft field takeoff involving Diamond Aircraft Industries DA20 aircraft; began to depart from Runway XX; by practicing a simulated soft field takeoff. On board the aircraft were an instructor and student. The primary focus of this dual exercise was for the student to refine the skills needed to perform a simulated soft field takeoff required as a private pilot task for FAA-S-ACS-6B. Prior to the flight the instructor thoroughly briefed the student on the proper exchange of flight controls through several exercises and it was clear to the student. After practicing the takeoff the first time; where the student made the mistake of keeping the stick fully aft; instead of slowly reducing back pressure once in ground effect; the student kept the stick in a full aft position creating a takeoff stall. The instructor was able to recover the aircraft by taking the controls and breaking the stall by lowering the angle of attack and regaining airspeed appropriate for a positive rate of climb. After the unsatisfactory performance of the soft field takeoff; the instructor decided to give the student another chance exercising a simulated soft field takeoff after completing several traffic patterns. Prior to taxiing Runway XX for takeoff the instructor asked the student how are you going to perform the soft field takeoff.  The student responded with the proper procedure and the instructor reminded the student of his mistake last time he attempted a soft field takeoff. The student properly taxied to runway centerline using constant back pressure on the stick and increased throttle to full power.  The student then used the proper right rudder pressure to compensate for P-factor. Once 500 feet down the runway; the airplane was able to get into ground effect however the aircraft was too slow pitch for Vx and after the instructor stated 'release the back pressure slowly' the student increased the pitch up and kept constant right rudder (stalling the airplane again). At this point the instructor took the controls and said abruptly 'my flight controls!' twice. The student failed to positively exchange flight controls to the instructor and locking the grip and control inputs contrary to the instructors. This lead to the plane striking the right wing on the runway pointing and losing control of the aircraft over the grass field to the right of Runway XX.  The instructor then overpowered the students control movements to counter a possible cartwheeling right prop strike; banked left while reducing the throttle to idle which caused the airplane to strike its left wing on the grass where it landed.  The instructor immediately secured the aircraft; preventing any chances of an onboard fire. Both the student and instructor survived with no injuries. It is unclear what total damage was done to the plane however there was visible damage to both wings.,,,,DA-20 Instructor reported a communication breakdown with student during a takeoff training event resulting in a runway excursion and ground strike.
1767378,202010,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,,Training,,Takeoff / Launch,,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,IFR,,,Landing,,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 100; Flight Crew Total 560; Flight Crew Type 536,,Communication Breakdown; Workload; Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Confusion,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1767378,Facility ZZZ.Tower,,Government,Local,Air Traffic Control Fully Certified,Air Traffic Control Time Certified In Pos 1 (yrs) 6,,Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction; Workload,Party1 ATC; Party2 Flight Crew,,1767419,ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Runway,,,Person Air Traffic Control,In-flight; Taxi,Air Traffic Control Issued New Clearance; Flight Crew Returned To Clearance,Procedure; Environment - Non Weather Related; Human Factors,Human Factors,I was conducting a flight training event with my student pilot. We just returned to the airport to practice performance takeoff and landings. We had just made a full stop - taxi back. We called holding short that we were ready for touch and goes. We were told to hold short for landing traffic. Several planes land and depart. Both my student and I hear what we believe to be our abbreviated tail number being cleared for takeoff. We read back cleared for takeoff instructions; finish final items on the checklist; and take the runway. On our takeoff roll we hear Tower ask who is on the runway and I respond with our tail number. Tower then advises to either exit the runway or begin our roll. We were already on the roll; so we continued the takeoff. After our lap in the pattern we terminate the training flight and contact the ATC number. I believe I heard our tail number and believed it was a takeoff clearance. However; due to a high volume of traffic the morning of the event due to a lengthy TFR that lasted most of the day; there was a lot of training and jet traffic. I could have heard a similar call sign and my student could have stepped on the intended recipient of the ATC instruction. I know when there is a high volume of traffic waiting to arrive and depart it could be best to use my full tail number to lessen confusion; and take extra measures to ensure all radio communications are properly received and copied.,,Aircraft X called up requesting pattern work during a high traffic volume session and was given hold short instructions; due to the fact that there was an IFR arrival jet on about a 3 or 4 mile final. Aircraft X subsequently read back his hold short instructions. I talk to 3 different aircraft before I cleared Aircraft Y for a touch and go. Apparently Aircraft X read back 'Aircraft X cleared touch and go' and then subsequently got onto the runway without me catching it. Aircraft Y clarifies their touch and go clearance and I canceled the touch and go clearance and gave them a left 360. During this time inside the cab my CIC/GC/FD was trying to clarify information about a TFR that was supposed to be going into effect shortly and we had received no prior information on. This resulted in several phones ringing during this already busy time. After scanning the runway I saw an aircraft who appeared to be holding on the runway with my jet traffic now within 2 miles of the runway; since I had multiple aircraft holding short of the runway I tried to quickly identify the aircraft; so I could taxi them off the runway in a timely manner. However Aircraft X didn't identify himself by name until about the 3rd time I reached out to them. With minimum time to react I told the aircraft to taxi clear of the runway or depart immediately. Aircraft X started their departure roll and as soon as airborne I told them to offset the runway so I had sufficient spacing with my IFR aircraft on final. Immediately following my Jet traffic landing the OM entered the cab and started trying to have the CIC help him find our local weather form; so our new trainee could fill it out. We started the day short staffed with no prior knowledge that someone would be coming in to cover for a couple hours; so the rotation wasn't going to happen as expected. When there are less people in the cab we have enough space to work without our masks and due to the fact that there were extra nonessential people in the cab I had to replace my mask; while I firmly believe mask should be required; they do interfere with the side tone which affected my ability to catch Aircraft X's incorrect readback. No one in the facility had received any information on the TFR that was supposed to be going into effect. This resulted in several miscommunications and confusion.,,Flight Instructor and Local Controller reported the instructor's flight departed without clearance with traffic on very short final after mistakenly taking another aircraft's clearance for takeoff.
1767961,202010,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,250,1,700,,,VMC,Haze / Smoke; 8,,Daylight,,,,FBO,DA40 Diamond Star,,,Part 91,None,Training,,Initial Climb,None,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Skylane 182/RG Turbo Skylane/RG,,,Part 91,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 56; Flight Crew Total 1190; Flight Crew Type 1100,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1767961,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC,Horizontal 400; Vertical 50,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was training my student in uncontrolled airfield operations and emergency landings. We were departing Runway 25 when I heard Aircraft X call that they were in the upwind for Runway 25. As the plane was about to rotate I asked where the Aircraft X was and they confirmed in the upwind. I cleared the whole upwind as we climbed and I could not find the plane. I remembered that my plane has TCAS and switched to the map to find the plane. I saw that he was 400 ft. away and slightly above me and at my 4 o'clock and flying right towards me and overtaking my aircraft. I then heard the Aircraft X call that he was entering left crosswind for 25. I immediately radioed 'Aircraft X; we are on a collision course; change course to fly over midfield immediately'. There are towers and hills on Runway 25's departure so I was limited in my options to take evasive action. Someone who I assumed was a flight instructor called 'roger Aircraft X crossing midfield'. I [saw] the plane at my 5 o'clock turn away from my aircraft towards midfield as we climbed and attempted to get out of the way.,,,,An instructor flying a DA40 reported a NMAC on initial climb from a Cessna 182 in the pattern.

1769994,202011,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,,,,Personal,PA-28 Cherokee/Archer/Dakota/Pillan/Warrior,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,Visual Approach,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Single Pilot; Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Student,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 20; Flight Crew Total 57; Flight Crew Type 25,,Human-Machine Interface,,,1769994,,,,,,,,,,,,Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Regained Aircraft Control; General Flight Cancelled / Delayed; General Maintenance Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,This is my second solo cross country of the day. I went to ZZZ1; ZZZ2 and back to ZZZ. Landings in ZZZ1 and ZZZ2 were good. Final was stabilized and right as the wheels were going to touch to ground the airplane yawed to the right. 1770386,202011,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,120,,CTAF ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,None,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Hangar / Base,,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 130; Flight Crew Total 1250; Flight Crew Type 1100,,Communication Breakdown,Party1 Other; Party2 Flight Crew,,1770386,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Object; Ground Excursion Runway,,N,Person Other Person,,General None Reported / Taken,Human Factors,Human Factors,My student was on his first solo flight while during his last landing he thought he was touch and go. I saw him touch down then raise the flaps; at that point I radioed to him full stop. I did not hear him add power but he said he did for another touch and go then upon hearing me he took the power out and preceded to stop. He locked down the brakes; the skid mark begins at the 1;000 ft marker on the other end of the runway. He was harder on the right brake than the left which caused him to skid off the right side of the runway. Which led him to strike a taxiway light with the propeller; the skid caused the right main landing gear tire to lose air and come off the rim. Then came to a complete stop.,,,,Flight Instructor reported the first time solo student pilot lost control of the aircraft during landing.

1771434,202011,0601-1200,AUO.Airport,AL,,3,,1700,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,CTAF AUO,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Part 91,None,Training,Localizer/Glideslope/ILS 36,Final Approach,,Class E ZTL,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,CTAF AUO,,Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng,,,,IFR,Passenger,Localizer/Glideslope/ILS 36,Final Approach,Direct,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 67; Flight Crew Total 1373; Flight Crew Type 297,,Situational Awareness,,,1771434,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC,Horizontal 200; Vertical 300,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,[We] departed AUO to complete a Commercial Pilot Stage Check. The objective was to complete a practice ILS approach to Runway 36 at AUO; with simulated vectors to the final approach course. The private; instrument rated pilot was the pilot flying (PF). He was wearing view limiting 'foggles'. The aircraft is equipped with an ADS-B traffic awareness system; displayed on the MFD. We were established on the localizer for Runway 36 at approximately 9 miles from the runway. The PF made his initial radio call on CTAF that we were 9 mile south on the ILS Runway 36. There was one other aircraft approximately 3 miles ahead of us; on final; on the ILS as well. We were approximately a 6 mile final when [Aircraft Y] reported 10 miles straight in for Runway 36. We subsequently made another distance call to alert the Aircraft Y of our location. By this time; we had the aircraft on the ADS-B display. That aircraft was at a higher altitude but substantially faster than our final approach speed of 90 KIAS. We had no visual contact with the Aircraft Y; our only reference was the track on our MFD. When he called 5 mile final; I asked over CTAF if he intended to overfly us on final. The response was; 'we will sidestep to the left'. When the ADS-B showed +300 and very close behind us; I stated to the student 'I have the flight controls' and descended and banked right. The pilot of the jet stated that he had us in sight no factor. We then saw the Aircraft Y slightly below and to our left as he passed by. The other aircraft ahead of us called low approach only and went around. We sidestepped to the right and climbed back to pattern altitude on an upwind leg. The Aircraft Y landed without further incident.,,,,Instructor pilot reported an NMAC on approach to AUO airport.
1771440,202011,1201-1800,SEE.Airport,CA,090,0.5,,1400,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,Tower SEE,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Initial Climb,,Class D SEE,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower SEE,,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Part 91,None,,,Initial Approach,,Class D SEE,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 210; Flight Crew Total 1214; Flight Crew Type 1000,,Situational Awareness,,,1771440,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC,Horizontal 100; Vertical 0,,Person Flight Crew; Person Air Traffic Control,In-flight,Air Traffic Control Issued New Clearance,Human Factors,Human Factors,I am writing this report to report a near miss situation in the standard traffic pattern for Runway 27L at Gillespie Field. My student and I were practicing traffic pattern operations at SEE. After checking upwind ; crosswind; downwind; clear we made a left turn into the pattern for Runway 27L. When my student looked to check the distance from aircraft to [the] runway; he also looked back and noticed that there was another aircraft right on our tail - same altitude; less than 100 feet behind us - same altitude. Tower advised that [he] was too close to us and told them to offset to the south for spacing. Aircraft Y offset to the south towards our 5 o'clock position and we got cleared to land #2 for Runway 27L.,,,,Instructor pilot reported an NMAC in the pattern at SEE airport.

1771766,202011,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,,1200,,VMC,10,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Champion Citabria 7ECA,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,,Other Downwind,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Champion Citabria 7ECA,,,Part 91,None,Training,,,Other Extended Downwind,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Gate / Ramp / Line,,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 100; Flight Crew Total 375; Flight Crew Type 270,,Other / Unknown; Training / Qualification,,,1771766,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Student,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 29.5; Flight Crew Total 29.5; Flight Crew Type 29.5,,Distraction; Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Confusion,,,1771780,Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance,,,Person Flight Crew; Person Observer,In-flight,Air Traffic Control Issued New Clearance; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors; Procedure,Human Factors,I am a flight instructor I was on the ground observing the traffic pattern. I had just sent my student on his first solo flight. There were three Citabrias in the pattern; all same company. My solo student was Aircraft X. Aircraft Z was on ½ mile final. Aircraft Y was on an extended downwind. My student; Aircraft X; was abeam midfield in the downwind. All traffic was in a left pattern. Tower called and told my student 'traffic to follow ahead in the downwind'. My student replied with 'traffic in sight'. My student had mistaken Aircraft Z on final as the traffic he was following; instead and of seeing and following Aircraft Y in the downwind. Tower proceeded to clear my student 'follow that traffic; clear to land Runway XX'. Because my student was following the wrong aircraft; he turned base (about a half mile) in front of Aircraft Y and cut him off. Aircraft Y was on a 1 mile final at the time. Aircraft Y saw the error and made appropriate maneuvers. Tower noticed when Aircraft X had turned final in front of Aircraft Y and proceeded to tell both aircraft to go around. No further events took place. The pilot in Aircraft X did not see or follow the correct traffic and turned base accordingly. He unintentionally deviated from the ATC clearance. The plot of Aircraft Y noticed and took evasive actions as necessary. I was on the ground and all distances are highly estimated.,,I was given traffic information by ATC while on downwind leg of pattern; a Aircraft X in the pattern ahead and to my left. I saw an aircraft matching ATC description on short final approach and responded that I had the traffic in sight. ATC gave landing clearance with instructions to follow that aircraft; so when I had sufficient distance behind I began my turn to the base leg of the pattern. Upon turning I spotted another aircraft ahead and to my right at about 500 feet clearance on final approach. I took a hard left turn to evade and was told by ATC to go around and that the aircraft I flew in front of was the traffic I was originally advised of and that I had cut them off. I continued in the traffic pattern and landed without further incident.,,A Flight Instructor observing from the ground and their student reported the student turned base leg and followed the wrong aircraft causing a subsequent aircraft to take evasive action.

1773419,202011,1801-2400,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,,Other Flying Club,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,1,Part 91,,Other Flight club,,,,,N,,,,Scheduled Maintenance,Inspection,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Other Exterior,FBO,Other / Unknown,Maintenance Airframe; Maintenance Powerplant,Maintenance Technician 30,,Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Training / Qualification,Party1 Maintenance; Party2 Maintenance,,1773419,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance,,N,Person Other Person,Other Logbook review,General Flight Cancelled / Delayed; General Maintenance Action,Aircraft; Human Factors; Procedure; Incorrect / Not Installed / Unavailable Part,Human Factors,I own a Cessna 172N that I lease to a flying club here. The club president and I agreed we would comply with 100hr inspections for reasons of safety due to the amount of flying the aircraft did. We did not think the 100hr was a requirement and did get clarification from the FSDO about this but still had them accomplished but with the thought that they were not required. This led to 2 overfly events for AD Date. I did not keep the logbook nor did I pour over it until just recently. It was kept in a locked closet where the club operates. I have changed a main ship's battery and a tire and some oil changes prior to Year but overall I wanted an Inspection Authority to work on the aircraft and wanted to stay out of the maintenance side. I had always thought it's better to get an unaffiliated outside person to perform the maintenance and annuals instead of someone that actively flys the plane and is the owner and club member. I think that the focus was on completing the 100hrs as an added safety measure but we did not notice that the seat rail AD was a 100hr requirement. Because of this if the Inspection Authority was not available or we were unable to move the aircraft for some reason it kept flying. I really did not know much of what was going on with the day to day schedule especially at the end of Year and on into Year/Year until now. I could not obtain my Class 3 MED due to a [medical issue] and quit flying all together for over X years. I kind of left it up to the club. Just recently I've taken advantage of Basic MED and am flying again. I had installed a broken piece of plastic on the elevator and while signing it off went back through the book. This is where I found the errors. On 2 occasions we flew past the seat rail AD once by 53hr and once by 11.6hr. The seat rail has now current with 6 hours remaining; we have scheduled the AD to be accomplished this week and will be well within the 100hr time limit. Going forward we have a clear plastic book onboard with all the inspections and their due dates and times. The club president is now aware that the 100hr is hard time and will schedule early going forward. We are prepared to ground the aircraft if we are unable to schedule with the Inspection Authority and I'm working on gaining access to the locked closet area where the logbooks are kept. At this time the seat rail is in compliance with the AD and will not overfly ever again. Thank you.,,,,Reporter described AD overflights due to errors and incorrect data entry into a commercial maintenance tracking program.

As practicing the landing I was told to pull quickly for the flare process of the plane and caused a miscommunication as to pull on the yolk quicker. With the miscommunication caused the airplane to balloon and land on the nose wheel hard and causing internal damage to the nose wheel internals; ripping almost all the screws off the nose wheel screws keeping it attached to the plane. After the incident the instructor took control of the plane and went on a go-around and landed the plane with the nose being as high off ground as possible.,,I was instructing my student on landing; focusing on the timing of flaring. He flared too much; which made him balloon. And to correct for it; he pushed down on the control to bring the nose down and landed nose first. The process was too quick for me to intervene. I heard a cracking sound as the nose wheel touched down on the runway. I executed a go around and made a soft field landing; wheelbarrowing the plane all the way down to the taxiway connected to our flight school's entrance. When I exited the plane; I visibly verified that the nose strut was sitting abnormally. I alerted our maintenance tech; who has verified that the nose strut was damaged.,,C172 student and instructor pilots reported a hard landing.

1776730,202012,0601-1200,SNA.Tower,CA,,,600,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,Tower SNA,FBO,PA-28 Cherokee/Archer/Dakota/Pillan/Warrior,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Initial Climb,Other traffic pattern,Class C SNA,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower SNA,,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,1,,,Training,,Initial Climb,Other traffic pattern,Class C SNA,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Single Pilot; Instructor; Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 40; Flight Crew Total 1000,,Situational Awareness,,,1776730,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC,Horizontal 300,,Person Flight Crew; Person Air Traffic Control,In-flight,Air Traffic Control Issued Advisory / Alert; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,A near midair collision occurred while in the traffic pattern. I was cleared to take off after [a] Cessna and was told to follow traffic. I took off and turned to John Wayne's standard 15 degree offset heading while climbing to TPA. Around 500 feet AGL I realized I no longer had traffic to follow in sight. I heard the Cessna request a short approach and ATC approved [him] for a short approach and clearance to land [Runway] 20L; after this I assumed that the traffic to follow was downwind and that I would have visual contact if I turned towards crosswind and downwind. As I was in the turn ATC asked me if I had traffic to follow in sight still. I reported back that I no longer had traffic in sight. ATC then told me to just fly a wide downwind for spacing. At this point the Cessna reported that [they] needed to make a right turn to avoid me. This whole time the Cessna was not in my visual; so they must have been beneath us and out of line-of-sight. I can only speculate on how exactly we converged as I had zero visual reference at this point with the Cessna. The Cessna and I continued flying the pattern together with no further incident but I did notice this Cessna was not flying the standard 15 degree offset on upwind and seemingly a little lower than TPA. I am unsure if this was an attributing factor to the loss of separation we encountered.,,,,PA28 Instructor Pilot reported an NMAC in the traffic pattern at SNA airport.
1776731,202012,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,,,CTAF ZZZ,FBO,Piper Single Undifferentiated or Other Model,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,Direct,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Air Transport Pilot (ATP); Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine; Other Seaplane and Glider,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 200; Flight Crew Total 2100; Flight Crew Type 120,,Training / Qualification,,,1776731,,,,,,,,,,,,Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Regained Aircraft Control,Human Factors,Human Factors,During a tailwheel transition training flight; the aircraft departed the runway surface on landing. The winds upon time of landing favored Runway XX and a right-crosswind component of about 10 knots was present at the time of the occurrence. No other traffic was in the pattern and the approach was stable throughout. The touchdown was in a three point attitude and did not bounce. On the rollout; the student improperly managed rudder control and the aircraft rapidly developed a significant turn to the left. As Instructor; I took control of the aircraft and stopped the ground loop from further developing. The aircraft departed the hard surface of the runway at roughly a 10 degree angle at a fairly slow speed and came to rest in the grass about 20 feet from the edge of the runway. Upon shutting the airplane down; both the student and I exited the airplane to assess the situation. No signage or lighting was hit nor was there any damage present on the airplane. The grass was smooth and no holes were present.The situation developed from a normal crosswind landing to a runway excursion quickly. The cause was an improper control input by the student that was not caught in time by me; the instructor. Despite not reacting in time to prevent the excursion; the aircraft did not ground loop and no damage was sustained by the airplane. Any corrective action would be on my part as the Instructor; to take control sooner before such a significant turn could develop.,,,,PA-12 Instructor Pilot reported his student lost directional control on the landing roll resulting in a runway excursion.
1778045,202012,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,280,3,,1300,,VMC,20,,Daylight,4500,,Tower ZZZ,Personal,Small Aircraft,,2,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Initial Approach,Other left downwind,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ZZZ,Government,Helicopter,,2,Other unknown,VFR,Other Pursuit,,Cruise,,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 208; Flight Crew Total 1473; Flight Crew Type 1291,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1778045,,,,,,,,,,,,ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Environment - Non Weather Related; Human Factors,Human Factors,After two right 360s we were told to extend downwind for runway X; and look for helicopter traffic (Aircraft Y) three miles west of the field at 700 feet. We called out traffic in sight; and continued. After Aircraft Y didn't respond to two radio calls; we were told to do another 360. Rolling out of the 360 we were told to look for Aircraft Y one mile ahead at 900 feet orbiting. We called traffic in sight; and began a climb to 1;300 feet. It appeared as though Aircraft Y was still climbing as they passed in front from our left to right. After a controller change; Tower called our position to Aircraft Y; they did not respond. Shortly after that call; Aircraft Y made a sharp climbing right turn directly into our flight path. To avoid a collision; I took the controls and made a climbing left turn as sharp as I could. Shortly after I started that turn; Aircraft Y banked sharply to their right to avoid us. I can't put an exact number on the distance between us; but it was close enough that I felt the need to bank sharply towards traffic on final; and Aircraft Y banked hard enough for us to see the bottom of their helicopter. Once a safe distance away; we turned to rejoin downwind; and began a descent back to pattern altitude. After that; Aircraft Y asked tower to keep aircraft away from that area while they followed a pursuit. Hearing other aircraft have difficulty with separation; we departed the pattern to ZZZ1 to avoid a similar situation.It is normal for us to fly over helicopter operations at 500-600 feet while in the pattern at 1;100 feet. It is not normal to fly the pattern with unpredictable traffic at the same altitude.,,,,Flight Instructor reported a NMAC with a helicopter.
1778369,202012,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,12000,,CTAF ZZZ,Personal,Small Aircraft,,1,Part 91,VFR,Ferry / Re-Positioning,,Takeoff / Launch,Direct,Class E Y; Class G Y,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Single Pilot; Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 1.5; Flight Crew Total 260,,Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure,,,1778369,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR,,N,Person Flight Crew,Other after mission,General None Reported / Taken,Environment - Non Weather Related; Human Factors,Human Factors,Due to the COVID pandemic; I have not been able to fly as much but had ample time in full motion jet simulators within the preceding month. That day I was working at the airport when I was contacted to help move planes around in the area for a business because their main pilot did not show up. I was told I was to be flown to an airport and to pick up a plane from a local airport and to fly to another airport. I got to the airplane and was able to fly the airplane to ZZZ. Upon arrival at the airport; the person I was following then asked for a ride back to the origin airport on the plane I was in. I accepted and flew without incident to the airport and made a safe landing. Upon landing; I realized that I had not been passenger current for single-engine aircraft. I would not say there was a lack of proficiency; just a lack of currency. I have been in and out of simulators for jets and had no worries that I could not fly and land the aircraft safely. I was just not able to fly as often as I'd like. I think some of the main causes of this was the fact that this was sprung on me with little warning and no clear plan and I had not flown with this group of people before. It was a major complacency incident on my part and lack of proper flight planning.,,,,GA pilot reported flying with a passenger while not being passenger current for single-engine aircraft.

1778822,202012,0601-1200,ORL.Airport,FL,253,1,,800,,Marginal,10,,Daylight,2300,,Tower ORL,FBO,Small Aircraft,,1,Part 91,None,Training,GPS,Initial Climb,None,Class D ORL,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ORL,,Small Aircraft,,1,Part 91,None,Training,GPS,,,Class D ORL,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 139; Flight Crew Total 1248; Flight Crew Type 501,,Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1778822,,,,,,,,,,,,ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC,Horizontal 200; Vertical 150,,Automation Aircraft TA; Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,The incident occurred while on the initial climb from runway 25 at Orlando Executive Airport (ORL). The probable cause appears to be communication and pilot error. Our aircraft was a Aircraft X. The student and I were remaining in the pattern practicing touch and go landings. An Aircraft Y [faster aircraft] was following us throughout the pattern. Our call sign was occasionally [mis-stated] which contributed to the confusion. During our pattern practice we were told to extend our downwind and that Tower would call our base. While we were in the right downwind and extended right downwind for Runway 25; Aircraft Y was noticeably gaining on us as shown on our MFD's traffic feature. Our base was approved and we were number 1 cleared for a touch and go Runway 25. [Aircraft Y] was cleared for a touched and go number 2 behind us. While on short final; it was noticeable once again on the MFD that Aircraft Y was gaining on us significantly. Our approach speed in the Aircraft X is 65 kts. With the headwind component that day our ground speed was undoubtedly slower than 65kts. Aircraft Y was told by Tower to do an s-turn on final for spacing as it was apparent they were getting close. The problem arose on the initial climb out following the touch and go; Aircraft Y overtook our aircraft while on the departure leg at approximately 800 feet; resulting in a near miss.The traffic we were following was told to extend upwind and we were expecting to receive a similar instruction for ourselves. The confusion seems to have begun when Executive Tower radioed for Aircraft Y to continue in the upwind and that they would call their crosswind. We did not respond to this call; as we assumed it was intended for Aircraft Y.  Aircraft Y responded confirming to extend their upwind until their crosswind was called. This transmission must have stepped on the Tower's transmission because as soon as Aircraft Y was finished broadcasting; the end of tower's transmission came through with the only audible portion being '...end upwind.' (Most likely 'extend upwind.')  This stepped-on call was most likely a follow up to [us]; but Aircraft Y then responded to continue their upwind for a 2nd time. Tower then called for Aircraft Y to extend their upwind. At this point the instructor in Aircraft Y; clearly confused; read back the extend upwind instruction for the 3rd time. We realized that the extend upwind call to [callsign] was most likely for us and we continued the upwind as instructed with the traffic ahead of and behind us being on extended upwinds.During this time; we again noticed Aircraft Y gaining on us on the MFD traffic. We continued in our upwind climb as Tower called for Aircraft Y to follow traffic ahead to the right (us). They responded that they had us in sight as they continued climbing and closing in on our left hand side. This is the approximate time that [we] was overtaken by Aircraft Y at approximately 800 feet MSL. Aircraft Y passed by us at roughly 200 feet off of our left wing; while both of us were still climbing to pattern altitude in the upwind leg.,,,,Instructor Pilot reported an NMAC on takeoff from ORL airport.
1781502,202101,1201-1800,1C9.Airport,CA,,,800,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,8000,,,FBO,Cessna 152,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Final Approach,None,Class G ZOA,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,CTAF 1CL9,,Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer,,,,,,,Final Approach,,Class G ZOA,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 40; Flight Crew Total 1600; Flight Crew Type 1550,,Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1781502,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Vertical 200,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was flying with a student pilot; practicing simulated engine failure emergency procedures. Student selected Frazier Lake airport (1C9) as the landing point. We positioned the airplane directly towards 1C9 for runway 5 which is a grass runway. I scanned the area in front and right of us to make sure there was no other traffic nearby. We descended towards runway 5 and ended the practice by going around above runway 5 at about 800 ft AGL. The next day we received a phone call from another pilot who was operating in traffic pattern at 1C9 attempting to land on the hard surface taxiway parallel to runway 5. He told us that he saw us on final flying next to him only approximately 200 ft above. He made few radio calls trying to reach us but no response; because we were not on 1C9 CTAF at the time. What have caused this event was that the student was busy performing the maneuver; forgot to change frequency to 1C9 CTAF and announce our intention. I was too focused on the training but overlooked the safety aspect of the flight. The corrective action is I should have changed frequency to 1C9 CTAF and monitor it when the student decided to head over there.,,,,C152 Instructor reported failure to utilize CTAF resulted in a NMAC on final.
1784342,202101,1201-1800,JNX.Airport,NC,,,0,,,,10,,Daylight,12000,,CTAF JNX,FBO,Small Aircraft,,2,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Takeoff / Launch,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,CTAF JNX,FBO,Small Aircraft,,2,Part 91,,Training,,Final Approach,,Class G JNX,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 125; Flight Crew Total 534; Flight Crew Type 232,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1784342,Aircraft Y,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 57; Flight Crew Total 1710; Flight Crew Type 1600,,Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1784326,Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical,Horizontal 6000; Vertical 500,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Airport; Human Factors,Human Factors,I was on the ground at JNX with my student pilot getting ready for a soft field takeoff. The pattern was very congested with 5 aircraft in the pattern in various places. An aircraft had just landed; and there were a few other aircraft on downwind. A downwind aircraft stated that they were extending their downwind for departing traffic. I told my student that after the landing aircraft had exited the runway to be ready for immediate departure. The exiting aircraft called clear at this point and I told my student to make the radio call and take us out. As we were taxing out the aircraft that had said they were extending downwind was now on a 1.5 mile final. I told the student to accelerate and a radio call over the CTAF said go-around. I took the controls from my student to avoid a confliction with the aircraft going around. The aircraft going around side stepped to the right to avoid conflict. At no time was a G1000 traffic advisory issued; and no aircraft came close to contact. The overpopulated pattern with 4 aircraft doing stop and goes and my aircraft trying to find a spot to get out was a contributing factor to this issue. After the aircraft sidestepped; they immediately departed the pattern; and we continued our takeoff and entered left closed traffic to continue landing practice.,,Myself and a student who is currently working toward his CFI certificate went out for a training flight. After an hour of practicing maneuvers we approached JNX to practice takeoffs and landings. During our final approach into landing on Runway 21 at JNX my student made a call to let the other traffic in the pattern know of our position and our intentions; shortly after this call another plane pulled out on to the runway in frontof us. We made the decision to go-around and commenced a turn to the west so not to be on a collision course with the downwind traffic. We then proceeded to climb and leave the area.,,GA instructors on different aircraft reported conflicting with each other at JNX non-towered airport.  Reportedly; one of the instructor's aircraft took the runway for takeoff as the other was on final prompting a go-around and sidestep to avoid a possible collision.  Traffic volume at the uncontrolled airfield was cited as a contributing factor.

Clearance was fly runway heading to intercept LAX 170 radial to LIMBO; V64; SLI; Direct. On departure from TOA my student was flying under the view-limiting device and I was pilot monitoring and looking outside for traffic. We departed Runway 29R; shortly after there was a departure from a parallel 29L of a light aircraft that was faster than our aircraft. While switching to Departure Control frequency we were advised of proximity of the overtaking aircraft and its altitude being same as ours. I was looking outside and was able to spot the aircraft in about 20 seconds and student flying advised ATC of us having visual contact. Another 20 seconds later I lost visual contact and took over controls momentarily using 3 step process to raise the left wing to check on the overtaking aircraft that was turning south at that time. I gave the controls back to my student using 3 step process. When my student was saying 'my controls' he blocked end of Controller's transmission for me. The part that I heard was only 'turn left 150.' Then; student read back 'Turn left 150 Aircraft X' and initiated a left turn to 150. At that time I started to question myself if this instruction could really be intended to us since it would probably put us below the MVA in the area. I clearly heard my student's readback to ATC about left turn to 150 and since Controller didn't say anything about his read back being wrong; I thought I shouldn't probably even worry. Just a moment later; because of the oddness of the situation I decided to clarify the instruction with the ATC; but by the time I was able to key the mic; Controller already was getting back to us questioning our actions. Only then I realized that my student responded to a call intended to another aircraft and Controller didn't even hear his readback because the transmission was blocked by the radio call of the aircraft that really received that instruction.I think contributing factors to this little misunderstanding was our scratchy radio. Because of it the student misheard the call sign and I couldn't even hear it; due to intercom on that particular plane being clearer than the radio and student was talking at the same time.Good thing there was no conflicting traffic and VMC conditions let me see the terrain.,,,,GA flight instructor reported a track heading deviation resulting in a CFTT event during departure from TOA airport.  Reporter stated they inadvertently took a heading clearance intended for another aircraft.

We were cleared for the option number 2 for Runway XX. Number 1 was on final and number 3 was student pilot solo who was behind us in the downwind after going around after his first landing attempt. We turned based and then to final being number 1. On about a 3/4-mile final from the runway; the student pilot solo turned base and then proceeded to turn final right in front of us; and slightly below us. My best guess is that he thought he was following number 1 and that he was number 2. At best glance; they were probably 400 feet in front of us; and 200 feet below us on final. I took flight controls; queried Tower and initiated a go around left side. The student landed and was given a phone number to copy down. After we completed our lesson a few laps around the pattern later and taxied off the runway; Tower asked if we were okay with the go around. It was certainly a little close for comfort; but we had enough space to recognize the threat and execute a go around.,,Was the 2nd solo flight in my pilot career. I had arrived back into ZZZ traffic pattern into Runway XX. While on downwind; I was cleared by Tower as number 3 and cleared to land on Runway XX. I had identified the traffic in front of me as number 2 without any doubt. I followed that traffic and landed safely. Once I called up ground; I was notified that I had cut off the actual number 2 traffic and that traffic was forced to go around. In reality; I had incorrectly identified the number 1 traffic as number 2 and failed to see any other traffic making me believe I had the correct number 2 in sight.When I am in a congested pattern like ZZZ; I will use my multi function flight display map page and make sure there are no planes I have failed to identify. I will also start counting out traffic to make sure I have accounted for all of them.,,GA flight instructor; a student on a solo flight; and the instructor of the solo student reported an NMAC in the traffic pattern during approach.
