1791775,202103,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,0.1,100,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,UNICOM ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Final Approach,Visual Approach,Class E ZZZ1,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 120; Flight Crew Total 1200; Flight Crew Type 900,,Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Ground Personnel,,1791775,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway,Horizontal 20; Vertical 100,N,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action; Flight Crew Executed Go Around / Missed Approach,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was acting as the instructor for a student pilot training flight. Myself and my student were in the traffic pattern for multiple touch and go's. There were several airplanes in the pattern; and as one aircraft was on the upwind; we had just turned final. About 400 feet following a standard 3 degree VASI (Visual Approach Slope Indicator); I noticed a truck moving from the ramp area toward our landing runway. I kept an eye on the truck and continued to work with my student. We made all standard radio calls on the CTAF; and all other traffic in the pattern were making consistent radio calls.As we continued our descent to land; the truck crossed the runway hold short line and entered the active runway. At this point; we were roughly 100 feet on short final. I instructed my student to go-around; as he was the pilot flying. My student made a timely go-around to avoid the truck that had entered the runway. I recognized the truck as being a hangar tenant for a private hangar located across the airport. The private hangars are not owned or rented by the airport's operator; and crossing the runway is one of two ways to access the hangars. The other access point does not involving crossing runways. The truck never made a call to cross via a handheld radio; and I don't believe the occupant of the truck was using any sort of radio to actively monitor the airport traffic before crossing the runway.,,,,An instructor pilot on short final at a non towered airport reported they ordered a go around when they observed a truck entering the runway
1792281,202103,1201-1800,IWA.Airport,AZ,,2,,2600,,VMC,10,,Daylight,CLR,10,Tower IWA,FBO,Small Aircraft,,1,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Initial Approach,Direct,Class D IWA,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower IWA,Personal,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,,,,,Initial Climb,,Class D IWA,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying; Single Pilot,Flight Crew Private,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 21; Flight Crew Total 121; Flight Crew Type 46,,Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1792281,,,,,,,,,,,,ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 0; Vertical 200,N,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Became Reoriented; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors; Procedure,Human Factors,Busy airport traffic pattern on [my] lesson solo. Multiple aircraft in traffic pattern of several different types. I was instructed to make left base for Runway 30L. I started to turn base without being cleared to land. Two aircraft; including myself and another aircraft which was on a very extended downwind south of the delta nearly 5 miles south of where I was turning 'base'; were instructed to make a right turn to re-enter the downwind to give landing space to an air carrier. I had never heard this command but interpreted it to mean to make a 360 back into the traffic pattern. Aircraft Y in front of me was given the instruction first and immediately started their turn to the right. When I was given the instruction; I waited to try to ask Gateway Tower what they meant; but the frequency was too busy. I decided to start the turn to the right to make a 360 to re-enter the downwind. Unfortunately; my slow thinking led to me making a turn at the same time that the aircraft in front of me was already almost finished with their turn. This resulted in a near head-on collision. The other aircraft fortunately realized this; pulled up and turned to their right promptly. I saw the aircraft fly over me and assumed it was an aircraft coming south from the gap with an odd pattern entry. Although a bit flustered; I was able to land the airplane and thought of it as a bad coincidence. The flight instructor on-board the other aircraft in the incident; approached me after my flight and asked to discuss once I returned. We discussed the incident and my flight instructor who was not on-board my solo flight; was also notified and joined us in the debrief.,,,,Student pilot reported confusion over ATC instructions during a solo flight in the traffic pattern. The pilot delayed a turn which resulted in a NMAC.

During the recovery phase of the quick stop; the student did not raise enough collective to arrest the descent. On the 45 to enter downwind on [Runway] 16; at approximately 1;100 ft. MSL (TPA 1;000 ft.); a turn in the opposite direction caused potential collision with traffic on crosswind turning to downwind.  Situation was realized simultaneously by Tower and myself (CFI) at which point I took [control of] the airplane; as I saw other planes in the base for [Runway] 16. 'Traffic to follow' was mis-identified. To avoid collision the turn was continued to the left; away from downwind; at which point Tower instructions to climb to 1;500 ft. MSL and proceed east to a known reporting point were followed.  Situation was stabilized; instructions from the Tower to re-enter the pattern for 16 were followed and successfully completed.What contributed to this situation:1) Student and CFI not adequately briefing the approach based on ATIS.  2) Not correctly identifying 'traffic to follow'.    3) Student Pilot did not realize she could ask for clarification or question my thinking.  4) I did not have the correct runway (16) approach visualized; I was distracted with coaching the Student Pilot.How to avoid in the future: Slow down the process to adequately brief the approach and ask for questions to understand that my student and I are thinking the same procedure with the given information.  Properly identifying the 'traffic to follow' and verifying with Tower.,,,,C172 Instructor Pilot reported an airborne conflict occurred in the traffic pattern when a 'follow traffic' clearance resulted in mis-identifying the aircraft to follow.

1799300,202103,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Other Part 141,None,Training,,Other All Phases,,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 40.5; Flight Crew Total 753.6,,Distraction,,,1799300,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,,,,,General None Reported / Taken,Procedure; Environment - Non Weather Related; Human Factors,Human Factors,I am a flight instructor at a 141 school. I am currently one of the instructors teaching the Private Pilot curriculum. The error I committed was sending one of my students on a solo flight without a current solo endorsement. Normally in our curriculum; a student pilot solo endorsement would not expire before the student earns their PPL. Due to COVID; our curriculum got pushed back and winter break put a pause on the private curriculum just a few flights before the check ride. The time added was enough for all student solo endorsements to expire. Knowing this; we added a reminder in our CFI guide that follows along with our Private Pilot Training Syllabus. The reminder was placed on the flight just before the solo flight. Due to the lost proficiency over winter break; I was not ready to give this student a new solo endorsement at the beginning of this spring semester.The issue began on the flight before the solo flight. This particular flight was the fourth time I had instructed this curricular period in the last 30 days so; I felt confident on the expectations of the flight. Because of this; I did not review the CFI guide before or after the flight and therefore missed the solo endorsement reminder. With my full permission; my student then flew solo the next day.I discovered the issue when I went to send that student on their next solo flight and I asked them to prove to me they had their required documents and endorsements. I then quickly gave a new solo endorsement.,,,,Flight Instructor reported a student flew a cross country flight without having the correct solo endorsement.
1799328,202104,0601-1200,JYO.Airport,VA,090,0.5,,1200,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,Tower JYO,FBO,Small Aircraft,,,Part 91,,Training,,Initial Approach,Other Pattern Operations,Class D JYO,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Small Aircraft,,,,,,,Initial Approach,,Class D JYO,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 50; Flight Crew Total 4000; Flight Crew Type 500,,Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1799328,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC,Horizontal 50; Vertical 20,,Automation Aircraft Other Automation; Person Flight Crew,In-flight,General None Reported / Taken,Human Factors,Human Factors,We were doing pattern operations at Leesburg with a student. We were on the left downwind for Runway 17 at Leesburg. It was busy with at least one other in the pattern and several aircraft waiting for takeoff and I believe two aircraft approaching for landing. About midfield I noticed on my portable ADS-B indicating an aircraft adjacent to us. Looking to the left there was an aircraft passing on our left just below and to our left. We were completely surprised by this. As far as I could tell the aircraft was doing a left downwind departure to the north which was unusual at Leesburg. I do not know if the aircraft had visual contact with us. Doubtful as we were in his blindspot. Most departures from 17 do a right hand departure to exit the pattern expeditiously. I heard nothing from the Tower that approved this and there was no warning from the Tower of the oncoming traffic. I confirmed with a fellow CFI in the pattern that I hadn't missed a call. 1800996,202104,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,0,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,4200,,Tower ZZZ,Personal,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,Visual Approach,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying; Single Pilot,Flight Crew Student,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 11.9; Flight Crew Total 22.7; Flight Crew Type 22.7,,Training / Qualification,,,1800996,,,,,,,,,,,,Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Aircraft Aircraft Damaged,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was taking off on my 3rd and final takeoff and landing for my first solo. I had 3 great landings with my instructor and had landed twice solo and was going in for my final takeoff and landing. I was climbing in the pattern and was at 800 feet when I turned right over [road] then leveled the wings. Waited 3 seconds and turned parallel to the runway at 1;100 feet. Powered to 4500 RPM got the clearance to land from Tower and radioed back for clear to land. I pulled the carb heat and when I got to ¾ of the runway I powered to 3000 RPM which is normal for a descent. I put in 2 seconds of flaps and took out the trim. I noticed I was a bit high at 900 feet when I turned over the shopping center so 100 feet above where I normally am. Put in some more flaps to about 20 degrees and turned in to final. I saw 3 whites and 1 red light; so I knew I was a bit high; I reduced power to get the plane to slow and reduce elevation. This gets me to the railroad tracks and descending in normally. Power is reduced to idle over the railroad tracks near Runway XX airplane starts to decent quicker than the last 2 times that I landed solo. As a result; I pitched up to get the glare shield on the horizon as that happened; I touched down and bounced on the runway. As the aircraft rose; I pitched for a decent angle thinking I was high above the runway; as the nose came over; I was surprised how close to the runway I was. Then I pitched for level flight; as I did this the aircraft touched down for a second; I thought It touched flat. But the nose dropped even more; this is when I heard the prop strike the runway. The aircraft went out of control veering to the left; as it departed the runway the nose gear collapses and digs into the dirt. The forward momentum of the airplane has the tail lifted off the ground before aggressively landing on the mains. the aircraft has come to a full stop; after stopping I paused for 3 seconds and then I contacted Tower and let them know what happened. After contacting Tower; I Opened my door and took off the seat belt; took the headset off and stepped out of the plan. I went out of the aircraft for 30 seconds before going back and turning the ignition off and turning off the master switch. After that I was met by airport ops.  After the initial shock and recuperating my thoughts I have found what mistakes I made on this solo and how this should have been avoided. Firstly; there is the initial bounce and when I caught air; I should have pushed into full power and pitched up to have the glare shield on the horizon which allows me to climb and then radio into Tower for a go-around. Definitely do not pitch down like I did and try to save the landing but rather go full power and pitch up for a climb. I was very appreciative of the airport ops and their quick action to make sure that I was safe and getting all the information to see how I didn't land correctly.,,,,GA student pilot reported a propeller strike during landing resulting in a runway excursion and nose gear collapse.
1801558,202104,1201-1800,FDK.Airport,MD,090,1.5,,1300,,VMC,10,,Daylight,10000,,Tower FDK,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Cruise,,Class D FDK,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower FDK,,Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer,,,Part 91,,,,,Direct,Class D FDK,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 170; Flight Crew Total 910; Flight Crew Type 654,,Situational Awareness,,,1801558,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance,Horizontal 50; Vertical 100,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,While in the traffic pattern at FDK; another plane that was cleared for takeoff and departing to the east; flew right into the traffic pattern that was in left pattern for the active runway. I recovered at about 400 feet AGL before climbing back into the traffic pattern.There isn't really a chain of events here; or a complex swiss cheese model; this was a reckless pilot who disregarded scanning for other aircraft and nearly collided with another.I've personally had two ATC directed; and three total (including this one) near misses within 2-3 nm of the field at FDK.,,,,Light aircraft Instructor Pilot reported an NMAC with another aircraft in the traffic pattern at FDK airport.
1802175,202104,0601-1200,GTU.Airport,TX,,,0,,,,6,,Daylight,CLR,,Tower GTU,Personal,Small Aircraft,,1,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Landing,Visual Approach,Class D GTU,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower GTU,,Small Aircraft,,,,,,,Landing,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,,FBO,Pilot Flying; Single Pilot,Flight Crew Student,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 32.8; Flight Crew Total 285.4; Flight Crew Type 285.4,,Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1802175,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance,Horizontal 600; Vertical 0,,Automation Air Traffic Control,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action; Flight Crew Executed Go Around / Missed Approach,Human Factors,Human Factors,I had just crossed the threshold for landing on Runway 18 when ATC announced 'Aircraft X on short final; go-around.' I had been cleared for landing as number three; with additional aircraft behind me; and had been directed to follow the Aircraft Y in front of me. In all previous communications; the Tower had used my tail number call sign. I heard ATC's call; but assumed that it was intended for the aircraft behind me since I was already well over the runway and ATC's previous calls had all used my call sign. I landed while the airplane in front of me was still on the runway; about 500-600 feet ahead. I heard ATC's direction; but assumed that it was for the airplane behind me and was concerned that climbing back in the pattern would put me in front of the other airplane that was going around. After landing; ATC gave me a phone number to call them and I did; explaining to them my perspective of the situation. As a student pilot; I had been told not to land when another airplane was on the runway; but failed to recall that during the landing because the round out was in progress and requiring my full attention. The experience of having to call the Tower and be reminded that I cannot land when another airplane is on the runway; irrespective of how far ahead that airplane may be; has burned the lesson into memory; and while I may make other errors; I will not repeat this one.,,,,GA student pilot reported landing while another aircraft was still on the runway at GTU airport.

1803113,202104,0601-1200,P08.Airport,AZ,,,0,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,UNICOM P08,Personal,Small Aircraft,,2,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Landing,None,Class G ZBQ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Small Aircraft,,,,,,,,,Class G ZBQ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 191.2; Flight Crew Total 1622.8; Flight Crew Type 1033.8,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1803113,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical,Horizontal 500; Vertical 0,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Environment - Non Weather Related; Human Factors,Human Factors,I was conducting instrument flight with a student flying a VOR approach circle to land. We were circling to land and making all appropriate radio calls for the circle. Both my student and I visually cleared the runway before touchdown. We were planning on doing a touch and go. After visually checking the runway and making two final calls; we touched down on the runway to conduct a touch and go. On the rollout when the student was getting ready to add full power; we saw an aircraft coming right towards us on their takeoff roll opposite direction down the runway. I immediately took controls from my student and got us off at the intersecting runway. The other aircraft realized what was happening and stopped as well. I made several attempts to contact the other aircraft with no response. We can only surmise that this aircraft rolled onto the runway while we were on a very short final leg and initiated a takeoff roll without checking to see if the area was clear; making a single radio call; or checking to see what other traffic was doing. The winds were heavily favoring the runway we landed on and there were several other aircraft using the same runway we were. I feel as though that there is nothing else that I could have done to prevent this other pilot from entering a runway and taking off opposite direction right into another aircraft.,,,,Flight instructor reported that during landing rollout another aircraft began takeoff roll from the opposite end of the runway without making any radio calls. 1804019,202104,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,289,5,,1800,,IMC,Rain; Turbulence; 2,,Daylight,1500,,TRACON ZZZ,Personal,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,1,Part 91,IFR,Training,GPS,Initial Approach,Vectors,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 124; Flight Crew Total 1380; Flight Crew Type 435,,Training / Qualification; Workload; Fatigue; Distraction; Confusion; Situational Awareness,,,1804019,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,Personal,Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Student,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 17.3; Flight Crew Total 277.1; Flight Crew Type 100,,Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload; Distraction; Confusion,,,1804065,Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence,,,Automation Air Traffic Control; Person Air Traffic Control,In-flight,Air Traffic Control Issued Advisory / Alert; Air Traffic Control Issued New Clearance; Air Traffic Control Provided Assistance; Flight Crew Became Reoriented; Flight Crew FLC complied w / Automation / Advisory,Human Factors; Procedure; Environment - Non Weather Related; Weather; Airspace Structure; Chart Or Publication,Human Factors,I was acting as a flight instructor on board Aircraft X; a Cessna 172S on a local IFR flight practicing approaches. My student is a Certified Flight Instructor (CFI) candidate who was gaining instrument currency and proficiency. We began with an ILS approach at ZZZ1 with my student flying the aircraft and me handling ATC communications to reduce his workload in the hard IMC conditions. We crossed a cold front while receiving vectors for the ILS approach where we encountered light to moderate turbulence and precipitation. We completed the ILS approach without incident and proceeded to the VOR for the VOR-A approach into ZZZ; planning to complete a Low Approach Only. We experienced severe turbulence which forced the autopilot (GFC700) to disconnect and I took the controls of the aircraft and requested deviations to the north as necessary to track clear of the progressing cold front. Once we got into smoother air; I gave my student the flight controls and we proceeded direct ZZZ2 [VOR] for a procedure turn. Our plan was to complete the VOR-A approach and then receive radar vectors for the RNAV 01 at ZZZ. My student had proclaimed that he wanted to avoid going back through the cold front while getting vectored for the RNAV 01 approach and suggested we circle to land at ZZZ and cancel the IFR flight plan. When my student suggested this; we had passed the Final Approach Fix inbound and began a descent to the Minimum Descent Altitude and were switched over to advisory frequency. I switched frequencies back to Approach to tell them our intentions to try and circle to land since they were expecting us to go missed on the practice approach. When I told ATC of our intentions; they replied in the affirmative and added 'Aircraft X; low altitude alert; check altitude immediately; altitude indicates 1;800.' I replied the altitude checks and requested an altimeter setting. ATC replied with an altimeter setting of 29.58 and we had a setting of 29.67 set in. I figured this was why they gave us the low altitude alert but then quickly realized that the Minimum Descent Altitude for the segment of the approach we were on was 2;020 feet and we were at 1;720 feet with the new altimeter setting. I informed my student to return to 2;020 feet and we continued on the approach without issue and proceeded with the missed approach with vectors to the RNAV01 at ZZZ. During the missed approach; I was surprised at myself that I did not catch that the student had descended below the Minimum Descent Altitude and I assessed why that had happened during a period of smooth flight and during the post flight discussion with my student. During the lead up to the approach; the encounter with the severe turbulence had shaken both me and my student. We also had a back seat passenger who was an instrument student who had never been in IMC before. I was concerned with the safety of my student and the back seat student and began thinking about the circle to land approach and how we would request vectors for the RNAV Approach if we were unable to circle to land in order to stay away from the front line. I had determined from the weather when we departed ZZZ that circling for the runway at ZZZ would have been nearly impossible with the current ceilings. I told my student this and informed him we would need to execute the RNAV Approach in order to make it back into the airport.The workload at the moment was very high and the effects of the turbulence certainly could have impaired multitasking skills for both my student and I. When we began the descent on the approach; we left 3;000 feet for 2;020 feet which is the Minimum Descent Altitude until a fix which then the Minimum Descent Altitude decreases to 1;760 feet. My student did not reset the altitude select when we ran our Final Approach Fix check and the altitude select remained at 3;000 feet. Additionally; when I recognized we were below the published Minimum Descent Altitude; I should have instructed my student to execute the missed approach as 91.175(E)(1)(i) states; rather than just climbing back up to the Minimum Descent Altitude.This flight was also my third flight in hard IMC this day; and this VOR approach was my 8th approach in IMC in a span of 6 hours. I am an experienced Flight Instructor with over 45 hours in actual instrument conditions and over 150 approach logged; but never before had I completed so many IMC flights in such a time span with the challenging conditions of the frontal passage. My self-assessment prior to this flight determined I was able to complete the flight successfully with good quality of instruction to the student; but the extraordinary conditions we experienced during the flight quickly eroded that ability for me; in addition to the highly divided workload situation we found ourselves in while inbound on the VOR Approach which led to the descent below Minimum Descent Altitude and failure to execute the missed approach immediately after. I think also a more comprehensive briefing of the approach would have aided in my student's short term memory of the initial difference of Minimum Descent Altitude. Even though I briefed the Minimum Descent Altitudes; I do not think they were retained due to the stress and workload of the situation. If this event were to occur again; I would better instruct my student to execute the missed approach rather than working to reclaim the missed Minimum Descent Altitude.,,The aircraft had 3 people on board for a local approaches flight in IMC conditions in Aircraft. This flight took place while a stationary front was passing through the area. This caused for almost constant moderate turbulence at times during the flight close to the frontal passage. The flight started with an ILS approach into ZZZ1. After the ILS approach we were vectored to go to the ZZZ2 VOR . Along the way; we had to deviate twice for turbulence. This; as well as IMC conditions; was causing a good amount of sensory overload for myself and the flight instructor with me. At times during the flight the autopilot was being used; but at one point; the amount of turbulence actually caused the autopilot to disengage. Because of this; at the time of the deviation; I was hand flying the aircraft while the other pilot was loading the VOR Approach. When we proceeded inbound on the approach; there is a step down to a minimum of 2;020 feet until an 8 DME fix. Then the minimum goes lower to 1;760 feet. With the sensory overload that both I and the other pilot were experiencing during the IMC flight; we ended up descending below the altitude minimum below the fix. ATC had not updated our altimeter setting in a decent amount of time. We were called by ATC letting us know for a low altitude and to immediately recover. They gave us an updated altimeter and our altitude after the correction showed it being right at the approach total minimum. Instead of executing an immediate missed approach we climbed back up to 2020 feet then re-descended to the 1;760 minimums. By doing this we unfortunately broke 14 CFR 91.175 (c) 1; 3 and (e) 1. The proper action would have been to either; not conduct the flight in the first place or; to immediately execute the missed approach once realizing the descent below the step down. We also could have stopped the flight after the ILS approach into ZZZ1. The rest of the flight utilized great CRM; but during this approach; a better action to even ask as the approach started would have been to double check the approach and its minimums including each step down.,,Instructor and student reported descending below Minimum Descent Altitude; which they attributed to an incorrect altimeter setting; and turbulence.
1805409,202105,0601-1200,SWO.Airport,OK,230,2,,2500,,VMC,10,,Daylight,12000,,Tower SWO,FBO,Small Aircraft,,2,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Initial Climb,Direct,Class D SWO,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,FBO,Small Aircraft,,,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Initial Approach,Direct,Class D SWO,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 103.0; Flight Crew Total 1091.9; Flight Crew Type 717.7,,Situational Awareness; Distraction; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1805409,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC,Horizontal 400; Vertical 0,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,The student and I had taken off of Runway 17 and at 1;500 feet MSL turned on course to the practice area on a heading of about 230. At this point; I had the student put on their foggles to start their simulated instrument time. Tower informed us that there was an aircraft about 6 miles to the South of the airport which was going in our general direction; their path was South to North. I acknowledged the call and told Tower we would keep a lookout for the traffic. The student asked about something on the instrument panels so I looked inside to answer their question. I heard the other aircraft radio that they had us insight. Since I had not yet gotten them in sight; I hoped to now be able to since they had. I looked back outside in the general direction that the airplane was supposed to be at (right side) and saw the airplane in a steep bank at approximately 400 feet from us with no vertical difference. As soon as I saw them; I banked the airplane to the right and kept our climb pitch attitude. I reported to Tower that I had the aircraft in sight.The conditions that caused the problem were: my heads-down time answering the student's question; not having Tower get a distance from the traffic; and not being able to locate them sooner.Actions to prevent/correct the situation: do not have my head down to answer a student's question; have Tower get a distance from the traffic.,,,,GA instructor pilot reported an NMAC during departure from SWO airport requiring an evasive maneuver.
1805426,202105,0601-1200,CVO.Airport,OR,,2,,400,,VMC,10,,Daylight,,,UNICOM CVO,,Small Aircraft,,2,Part 91,,Training,,Final Approach,Visual Approach,Class G CVO,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Small Aircraft,,,,,,,Final Approach,,Class G CVO,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 150; Flight Crew Total 805; Flight Crew Type 775,,Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1805426,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 2; Vertical 2,,Person Flight Crew; Person Observer,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was doing an instrument approach in to CVO with a student. RNAV 35. We had made normal radio calls; 10; 7; 5; 2 and 2 miles out.There was one plane in the downwind who had called #2; landing behind my student and I on Runway 35. When we were below the LPV minimums and the student had removed the foggles; somebody on the ground holding short of Runway 35 called out 'there is about to be a mid air collision for the 2 planes on final.'My student and I both were looking out straight ahead and to the sides and saw nothing. Out of nowhere a plane [Aircraft Y] came over the top of us; from behind and to our right and almost clipped our left wingtip.To our knowledge; there was only one plane in the downwind aside from us on short final and 2 planes holding short of 35 ready to depart. My student confirms that they saw Aircraft Y land on Runway 35 and taxi off with no radio calls.We did everything right; making all the appropriate radio calls. Aircraft Y made no calls and we never saw them on ADS-B or out the window. The pilots from on the ground from two different planes both confirmed that Aircraft Y made no radio calls and that I and my student were doing everything correctly.I never saw Aircraft Y visually or over ADS-B. The student was under the foggles for the approach but when he went visual; we still never saw a plane near us.I can confirm nobody was departing Runway 17 at the time because there was already 1 plane doing pattern work for 35; and the plane who called out the near midair collision from the ground; had just completed a taxi from 17 to 35 on the ground because it was the runway in use.This was within feet of hitting our wing from above. Not only was this incredibly unsafe; but the fact that no radio call was made ever is even more concerning.,,,,GA flight instructor reported an NMAC during final approach to CVO non-towered airport. 1805648,202105,0601-1200,JWG.Airport,OK,,,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,12000,,,FBO,Small Aircraft,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Final Approach; Landing,,Class G JWG,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Small Aircraft,,,,,,,Taxi,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Air Transport Pilot (ATP); Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 55; Flight Crew Total 1230; Flight Crew Type 28,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1805648,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Runway,Horizontal 1200; Vertical 0,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Executed Go Around / Missed Approach; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,Me and my student are on a cross country training flight from ZZZ to JWG on clear VMC day with light and variable winds. We are coming in from the east to enter the traffic pattern at JWG by flying over head the airport and entering the right downwind for Runway 17 as that runway is right traffic. Approaching overhead I notice that there are multiple aircraft taxiing on the ground on the parallel taxiway. We make multiple position reports on local CTAF about our position on each leg of the traffic pattern and me nor my student hear any other radio calls for our destination. The student is flying the entire traffic pattern and was doing a normal approach and landing. Our last radio call was on short final about one half to one mile final. As soon as we touched down on Runway 17 about 500 feet from the threshold; both me and my student notice that an aircraft [Aircraft Y] had pulled onto the runway from what appeared to be a taxiway that was at the midpoint of the runway and had turned to face north as if the aircraft had intentions to takeoff or back taxi on the runway. As soon as me and my student noticed the aircraft facing directly at us; about two seconds after touching the ground; my student executed a go-around and immediately climbed our aircraft away from the runway and made a slight turn to the left so that we would not overfly the runway. We then exited the traffic pattern back to ZZZ without further incident. This airport is a class G airport so there is no requirement for use of radios in that airspace; but there seemed to be little vigilance on the part of Aircraft Y for noticing an aircraft on short final with strobe and landing lights operable and on.,,,,GA Flight Instructor reported a conflict during landing at non-towered JWG airport. Reporter stated an aircraft had taxied on to their same landing runway requiring a go-around right after touching down.
1805892,202105,1201-1800,DED.Airport,FL,,,,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,,,CTAF DED,FBO,Small Aircraft,,2,Part 91,,Training,,Landing,,Class G DED,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer,,,,,,,Taxi,,Class G DED,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Total 643; Flight Crew Type 612,,Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1805892,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was the instructor with a student training for a private pilot check-ride. The runway in use was Runway 30. My student entered mid-field left downwind for Runway 30 and made all appropriate calls. For example 10 miles out; 5 miles out; entering mid-field left downwind; left base; and final on the CTAF frequency. As we turned base another aircraft took off and was climbing out as we turned final. When my student was coming in; student was preparing to do a soft field landing. There was also active parachuting going on. 1806477,202105,1201-1800,EBZW.Airport,FO,,,,1500,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,,FBO,Small Transport,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Initial Approach,Visual Approach,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Personal,Small Transport,,1,Part 91,None,Personal,,Initial Approach,Visual Approach,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Air Transport Pilot (ATP),Flight Crew Last 90 Days 89; Flight Crew Total 8500; Flight Crew Type 1500,,Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1806477,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR,Horizontal 120; Vertical 0,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Aircraft Equipment Problem Dissipated; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was doing training with the Aircraft X in the right hand seat as flight instructor; left hand seat occupied by experienced skydive pilot. During the final of the first touch and go of his session of 3L heard the Aircraft Y on the frequency asking landing information. I gave him 3L in use with right hand circuit and 2 aircraft doing touch and go training. When coming in right downwind again Runway 3L we got a traffic warning on the GPS screen. Traffic appeared to be head on 200 feet above. PIC didn't see it but I spotted the traffic head on almost same altitude and called the conflicting traffic to warn him being opposite in the downwind head on. He replied to join right downwind 3L. As PIC still couldn't see the traffic and a collision was going to happen I took the yoke and turned the aircraft to the right with a slight down input. Conflicting aircraft never saw us neither did any avoidance maneuver.PIC had back the controls and we did a second touch and go. Meanwhile the Aircraft Y joined the right downwind 3L and landed when we where again end of downwind. Turning on final for full stop ( final call was done) the Aircraft Y reported entering back track 3L. Being surprised as we where already on final I saw he could however vacate heaving 3 taxiways ahead. Nevertheless the pilot of the Aircraft Y called us that we better did a go-around as they would not be able to vacate in time. I replied that his behavior was very unprofessional; first positioning his aircraft opposite ours in a downwind leg and then entering and blocking the active runway with an aircraft on final. After we landed and shut down the aircraft I expected at least that the PIC of the Aircraft Y would come to apologize; but no one came to us. When checking the airport register I also noticed he never registered his inbound nor outbound flight.  When checking FlightRadar24 you can clearly see that the Aircraft Y flew opposite the downwind descending through 1;700 feet of the 03L to do a 180 turn to join his opposite track. The Aircraft X is at the same moment at 1;500 feet flying correct downwind position for the 3L. Closing speed was around 250 kts.,,,,Flight Instructor reported an NMAC event with during landing training followed by a ground conflict with same aircraft operating in a nonstandard manner.

1810347,202105,0601-1200,CPT.Airport,TX,,,0,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,CTAF CPT,Personal,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Takeoff / Launch,Direct,Class G CPT,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Personal,Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Taxi; Landing,,Class G CPT,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 200; Flight Crew Total 5800; Flight Crew Type 150,,Time Pressure,,,1810347,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 1,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,At Cleburne Regional Airport it is hard to see traffic on the other end of field due to center of runway being highest elevation. 1810360,202105,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,500,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,UNICOM ZZZ,FBO,Duchess 76,,2,Part 91,IFR,Training,,Takeoff / Launch,None,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Engine,,X,Malfunctioning,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 60; Flight Crew Total 1750; Flight Crew Type 100,,Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1810360,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 500; Vertical 500,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Landed As Precaution; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action; Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport; Flight Crew Overcame Equipment Problem; General Flight Cancelled / Delayed; General Maintenance Action,Aircraft; Human Factors,Human Factors,Flight for Part 141 Multi-Engine Instructor (MEI) applicant. Preflight was claimed complete; both instructor and student walked out to [the] airplane; started engines; and taxied out. Run-up was normal; as was taxi. On takeoff; engine checks were complete and in the green. Upon rotation and climbout; both oil temperatures and cylinder head temperatures were rising rapidly. At 500 feet; instructor told MEI student to return to airport; [the] temperatures were rising too fast. Lowered power output and maintained 700 feet AGL. By the end of the downwind; both temperatures were in the red; oil pressure still in the green. Base to final had normal airspeeds. Landed safely with engines operating.Upon landing and rollout to taxi; engines began to stutter. Mixtures were pulled as we exited the runway and airplane was shut down. Post-shutdown examination showed engine plugs were not taken out. Thus; pre-flight had not been completed. Engine malfunction was due to student not completing pre-flight and instructor placing too much responsibility and trust upon [the] student to complete such actions. It is the student's responsibility to complete the pre-flight; but the instructor's responsibility to ensure pre-flight is completed. Corrective action would be for instructor to check the MEI student's pre-flight responsibilities and checklist items.,,,,BE-76 flight instructor reported an engine temperature problem during takeoff resulting in a return to departure airport.
1810599,202105,1801-2400,ZZZ.Airport,US,,1,,600,,VMC,10,,Night,12000,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Cessna 152,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Initial Climb,,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ZZZ,Personal,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Initial Climb,,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying; Single Pilot; Trainee,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Private,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 30; Flight Crew Total 203; Flight Crew Type 177,,Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1810599,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC,Horizontal 0.1; Vertical 50,,Automation Air Traffic Control; Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was practicing traffic patterns at the airport (ZZZ) and when I was turning to the right crosswind; I noticed the plane behind me was already in the upwind. I thought he was going to extend his upwind to give me more space; so I continued normally. As soon as I joined the right downwind for Runway XXR; I heard Tower ask the other plane if he was still following the traffic in front of him; looked towards my right trying to find him and I saw him off my right wing doing a climbing left turn to get away from me.The tower did not tell the other pilot anything after that. I don't know if he did not see how close we were; or he thought it was irrelevant to say something. As for the other pilot; he must have been distracted and lost sight of me. I will be more aware of my surroundings next time. This happened before the tower closed. I am glad it was still controlled airspace; otherwise it would have been another (probably tragic) outcome.,,,,C152 reported an NMAC event during landing training.
1810616,202105,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,3800,,Tower ZZZ,Personal,Cessna 150,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,Visual Approach,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Company,,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 240; Flight Crew Total 1400; Flight Crew Type 100,,Training / Qualification; Confusion; Situational Awareness; Distraction,,,1810616,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,Personal,Trainee; Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Student,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 41; Flight Crew Total 133; Flight Crew Type 133,,Training / Qualification; Distraction; Confusion; Situational Awareness,,,1810620,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Regained Aircraft Control,Human Factors,Human Factors,According to my student: While he was doing solo touch/goes at ZZZ; on his second landing; he touched down left of centerline. While rolling with the throttle in the idle position; he turned off the carb heat and began to retract the flaps. The nose of the plane began to veer right. When he applied left rudder he said the plane felt as if it would skid; spin or drop the nose onto the ground. Therefore; he applied just enough left rudder to straighten the nose wheel and rolled onto the grass adjacent to the runway. No contact was made with any runway signage or lights. There was no damage to plane; runway; or grass area; and there were no injuries. Tower cleared for continued movement to the Alpha taxiway. He continued to the transient parking area and called ZZZ Tower per their instructions.As the instructor; my student called me to inform me he had run off the runway; no damage had occurred; and he had spoken with the tower and FAA. I did not know he was flying by himself that day and had received no notification from him. I asked him to recount what happened to me several times trying to understand what happened. I called the Tower and confirmed that the winds were variable at 3 knots and visibility was very good. Based on his recount; I do not fully understand how he thought going off the runway was his safest option. I have not offered him any training or instruction that would indicate that was good judgment. He has never landed far off centerline with me in the plane and has never demonstrated that he would ever act in such a way. He and I have logged extensive dual hours at ZZZ doing pattern work; and he has never flown in a way that indicated he would act or make a decision in this manner. He had demonstrated consistently with me that he was able to maintain directional control of the airplane both in the air and on the ground. I have informed him that all of his solo endorsements are no longer valid. I was planning to spend an extensive amount of time with him on the ground and in the air addressing what happened yesterday through re-training; but he has decided to discontinue his flight training at this time. As a result of this incident; I have re-clarified to all students that they must inform me of any time they plan to solo and must receive my permission before doing so. I have also implemented a strict rule of no solo touch and goes. Solo pattern work will from now on only be full stop landings.,,While doing solo touch/goes at ZZZ; on my second landing; I touched down just left of center. While rolling with the throttle in the idle position; I turned off the carb heat and began to retract the flaps. The nose of the plane began to veer right. Applying left rudder the plane felt as if it would skid; spin or drop the nose onto the ground and I was too far toward the edge of the runway. I felt it best; to reduce the chances of injury or damage. I applied just enough left rudder to straighten the nose movement and rolled onto the grass adjacent to the runway. No contact was made with any runway signage or lights. No damage to plane; runway or grass area and there were no injuries. Tower cleared for continued movement to the taxiway. I continued to the transient parking area and called ZZZ Tower per their instructions. As a result of this occurrence; training has been suspended for evaluation and scheduling with CFI.,,Instructor and student pilots reported the student experienced a runway excursion on landing rollout during a solo flight.

1815668,202106,0601-1200,VGT.Airport,NV,,,,2800,,,Smoke/Haze; 5,,Daylight,10000,,Tower VGT,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Part 91,VFR,Training; Other Check Ride,,Initial Climb,,Class D VGT,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower VGT,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Climb,,Class D VGT,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying; Single Pilot; With DPE,Flight Crew Student,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 30; Flight Crew Total 50; Flight Crew Type 50,,Distraction; Confusion,,,1815668,Aircraft Y,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 60; Flight Crew Total 445; Flight Crew Type 420,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew,,1815700,Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance,Horizontal 400; Vertical 200,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action; Flight Crew Became Reoriented,Human Factors,Human Factors,On initial climb out 600 ft. AGL; [an] airplane climbing from [the] parallel runway turned left crosswind in front of me with no ATC clearance; causing me to level off for collision avoidance. ATC was supposed to call our turns but the other aircraft did not follow instructions.,,I; [the] Flight Instructor; took a private pilot; whom I have never flown with before; up in the traffic pattern to 'kick off some rust' as he hadn't flown in the last 60 days. We had done 8 touch-and-go's prior and were completing one more to end the lesson. Upon takeoff; Tower called and stated; 'Aircraft Y continue upwind; I will call the crosswind.' We continued the upwind and I began talking with the private pilot to do the right traffic; etc. At this point; Tower called up to unknown aircraft and states; 'Turn left crosswind.' I did not hear the tail number clearly and could not confirm it was for our aircraft. [The] private pilot states the call was for us and was given to turn left crosswind. I stated I did not hear the call and cannot confirm. I began to second-guess him and asked 3 times; and each time the private pilot stated yes; we have the okay to turn left. [The] private pilot turns left and Tower called and stated; 'Aircraft Y; turn right crosswind.' [The] private pilot got on the mic and stated; 'We are in the wrong downwind and made the incorrect turn.' Other aircraft later transmits it was a 'close one' to Tower.To avoid this from happening in the future; I believe as Flight Instructor I should have called the Tower due to the miscommunication. At the end of the day; I have more experience and it is my duty to make sure the aircraft is operated correctly and safely. I also believe the private pilot should have recognized they were unsure of the radio call and [to] call to Tower as well. If the communication was better in the cockpit and we were more authoritative to speak with Tower; this situation could have been avoided.,,Pilot Flying in light aircraft and Private Pilot and Flight Instructor in another light aircraft reported encountring an NMAC with each other in the pattern after the latter misunderstood a clearance.

1815953,202106,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,1,1000,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Final Approach,Other Pattern work,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ZZZ,Other unknown,Small Aircraft,,1,Other unknown,,Other unknown,,Final Approach,,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Single Pilot,Flight Crew Private,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 0.9; Flight Crew Total 210; Flight Crew Type 210,,Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown; Confusion,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1815953,,,,,,,,,,,,ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Taxiway,Horizontal 5400; Vertical 0,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Air Traffic Control Issued Advisory / Alert; Flight Crew Became Reoriented; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,With just 0.9 hrs of PIC time YTD; I arrived at my flying club's towered home field; ZZZ; rested and eager to shake off some rust. My first sign of how much rust I had came when I accepted a Ground instruction to RWY XX but taxied to the nearer RWY XY. After completing my runup; Ground advised me to taxi to RWY XX. I thanked Ground for 'that catch' and received a double-click 'you're welcome.' I paused; ensured I was focused and not letting myself feel rushed; and proceeded to RWY XX. I completed four takeoffs and landings; and after reviewing LiveATC recordings I believe that my radio communications were professional and crisp. Ground did request that I confirm one hold-short instruction; and Tower asked that I confirm a 'give way to helicopter' instruction as part of a 'hold short' read back. However; I acknowledged and complied with all instructions promptly; including hold-shorts; midfield reports; extended down winds; go-arounds; no delay etc.; using proper phraseology. A midair near-miss occurred when two Cessna's with 'XXXX' in their call signs began to turn base at the same time -- Aircraft Y from Right Downwind; and I; Aircraft Z; from Left Downwind. I mistook a 'cleared for the option' instruction for Aircraft Y as being intended for me; and radioed my acceptance for a full stop. I believed Tower had cleared me to land. The conflicting traffic had been advised of 'that Cessna on Left Downwind;' from which I further inferred my own landing priority over this newcomer to the pattern. Upon review of the recordings; it is clear to me that Tower attempted to clarify that the landing clearance was for Aircraft Y; and that the call out to my position was purely advisory for Aircraft Y -- and not a reaffirmation of a clearance for Aircraft Z to land. However; someone stepped on the frequency; and I missed the clarification. It was only after Tower instructed me; 'You need to turn right now' that I saw the conflicting traffic approximately 1/2 mile turning right base. Tower then instructed me for the first time that I was #2 for the field. I attribute this near-miss primarily to my own lack of recency; but secondarily to additional factors. I lost situational awareness of other similarly-[call] signed Cessna's entering the pattern from the opposite direction. ATC could have clarified our landing sequence earlier; or verbally emphasized the differences in our call signs. (A minute later; Tower itself briefly confused two call signs; instructing me to turn Right Base when I was already on Short Final from Left Base; Tower quickly corrected itself when I advised of my position.) It was also a very busy pattern in which to shake off rust -- for pilots and ATC alike. Simultaneous radio transmissions obscured instructions that might otherwise have been sufficiently clear. Stress was apparent: After landing; I complied immediately with Tower's instruction to exit without delay -- only to be told urgently to 'stop right now' to avoid a jet on its takeoff roll. (I appreciate Tower's urgency: I had acknowledged the hold-short instruction and was already preparing to stop; but to their eyes I was still in 'no delay' mode as I transitioned from RWY to Taxiway.) Tower similarly expressed frustration with another pilot for requesting 'a turn around a point;' a term that Tower did not recognize; they doubtless would have preferred 'a 360' or 'a circle.' When I was finished with my pattern work; I briefly expressed my appreciation to Tower and received a friendly 'no problem' in response. I think we all did what we could to be as clear as possible (urgently if the situation demanded it); and to correct our mistakes. Although it will be frustrating at times; on balance I think this is a good set of attitudes to have; especially as the entire National Airspace System shakes off varying degrees of rust coming out of the pandemic. The dangers here were addressed; but a slightly more intransigent attitude; or a slightly more congested frequency; might have tipped the balance to a midair collision.,,,,A Single Light Aircraft Pilot; with low flight time because of the pandemic; reported a NMAC turning final after getting confused because of similar call signs. The Tower controller separated the aircraft and a normal landing was accomplished.
1815979,202106,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,0.5,700,,,VMC,Haze / Smoke; 10,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,2,Part 91,,Training,,Final Approach,Visual Approach,Class D RVS,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower RVS,FBO,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,,Training,,Final Approach,Visual Approach,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying; Trainee; Dual instruction flight,Flight Crew Student,,,Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1815979,,,,,,,,,,,,ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance,Horizontal 500; Vertical 200,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors; Procedure; Environment - Non Weather Related; Company Policy,Human Factors,The instructor and I were on a checkout flight in a flight school C172. After the training flight; we returned to ZZZ for 1 touch and go and 1 full stop landing. It was VFR conditions; but hazy with scattered clouds about 2000 feet above the airport. The airport was very busy with multiple training aircraft in the pattern using both runways. We were assigned Runway XXR. We completed our touch and go and were instructed to fly runway heading. After several minutes; we advised ZZZ Tower that we were still runway heading; at which point the controller advised us to turn right crosswind for right closed traffic to Runway XXR. While on the downwind; the controller advised us to extend downwind and he would call our base. We read back the instruction.When we were approximately .75 statute miles northwest of the airport; the controller changed our clearance to fly a close approach and we were cleared for the option. We read back the clearance and turned right base. Because we were high; we extended flaps to increase our descent rate. As I was about to turn final; the controller (a different voice this time) advised us to extend downwind; which we read back. I began an immediate climbing left turn. The controller immediately followed that clearance by clearing Aircraft Y to fly an immediate left 360. Aircraft Y was on final to either [Runway] XXL or XXR. There were multiple flight school aircraft with similar call signs in the pattern. Aircraft Y mistakenly made a right 360. I gained a visual contact on Aircraft Y; who was at my one o'clock low. I continued my left turn and climb to avoid collision with the aircraft. We extended downwind and were then given clearance to land. We landed without further incident. I believe that the hazy conditions; busy controllers; controller change or controller training; and multiple aircraft from the same flight school and similar call signs created confusion leading to this incident.,,,,Student Pilot reported a NMAC with another flight school aircraft with a similar sounding call sign which had turned the wrong direction.

I found them almost directly above and to my left making a left hand turn that was leading into our course. I immediately descended to approximately 150 AGL to build separation from the craft and turned to the right to avoid a collision course. I called out upon the radio to connect with the the other aircraft and no response was received from the other pilot; who I came to find out was a solo student. The plane was flying extremely tight patterns cutting off the flow of helicopter traffic that is typically flying on the adjacent taxiway.
