1826549,202107,1801-2400,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,200,,,VMC,,,Night,,,CTAF ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,Visual Approach,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,No Aircraft,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 156; Flight Crew Total 713; Flight Crew Type 129,,Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Ground Personnel,,1826549,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 100; Vertical 200,N,Person Flight Crew,Other crossing theshold,General None Reported / Taken,Environment - Non Weather Related; Human Factors,Human Factors,The runway incursion occurred when a new CFI and myself were doing a night flight for the said CFI to become night proficient again in small GA aircraft after not flying GA in a long time. ZZZ Tower had closed 30 minutes prior and we were the only aircraft working in the pattern. I said that we should practice a power off 180 when the incursion occurred. The situation that occurred was that Airport Operations was doing sweeps of the runway and either they did not announce they were on the runway or we did not hear them due to being focused on the power off 180 maneuver. As we turn from base to final and get closer to the runway; we did not see anything on the runway that would have warranted a go-around. As we start to line the aircraft up with the runway a few hundred feet above the ground we see on the very edge of the runway two sets of stationary lights that were on the edge that we initially mistook for runway edge lights; but by the time we were about to pass; we saw it was a vehicle. Being low to the ground; still in a bank; low energy; and with nothing in front of us I determined going-around was not the optimal decision to make since the vehicle was now behind us. After seeing it was a vehicle of some sort I initially believed that the sweeper had moved off into the grass; however the driver came over after we landed and said he was still on the runway. We landed 300 ft. past the vehicle to the best of my knowledge so there was no immediate concern for a collision.I believe that the situation would not have occurred had several things happened. A breakdown of communication had occurred in the chain of events between the aircraft and the Ground Operations in terms of knowing the position of where everyone was. We made a downwind call but did not make subsequent calls due to the high workload of the power off 180 maneuver. I cannot confirm if the ground vehicle did or did not make a call; but to the best of my knowledge they did not make the call saying they were on the runway.,,,,Instructor Pilot reported that during night VFR approach; the runway was being swept by a truck while the tower closed and there was no indication that the runway was closed.
1828075,202107,0001-0600,ZZZ.Airport,US,,0,0,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,2,Part 91,,Training,,Landing,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Trainee; Pilot Flying,,,,Training / Qualification,,,1828075,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 66; Flight Crew Total 337; Flight Crew Type 330,,,,,1828094,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence,,,Person Flight Crew,Other Landing,Flight Crew Regained Aircraft Control,Human Factors,Human Factors,While practicing short field landings; I came in on final at 70 kts. for Runway XX at ZZZ. I touched down on the runway with a slight right crosswind as I had done on the landing 5 or so minutes before; where I felt the same thing had happened; being only two of the three wheels initially touched. On the first landing this was not a problem and we took off again without issue; but during this approach I attempted to fix the problem by putting in right rudder as my Instructor told me to; which would have been fine if I had not also hit the right brake as well; causing the Aircraft to turn sharp to the right and drift sideways into the ditch between the runway and the taxiway. Both me and my Instructor were ok; and the plane seemed intact. My Instructor took the controls swiftly after we veered off course and maneuvered the plane gently into the ditch. After this we turned the engine off.,,I am a Flight Instructor and was practicing landings with my student. We were practicing short field landings and were inbound for the second landing at the airport. On final the student had made the remark we were coming in slightly fast and began correcting for the correct airspeeds. The approach to landing itself was not abnormal.  It was on centerline and at a proper glidepath; just slightly fast. Due to the fact that we had been practicing short field landings; the student was aiming to flare at a point that likely should have been extended. As we flared; a little bit of crosswind caused there to be a slight sideload on the left wheel and at the time it was the only wheel touching the ground. As the Instructor; I had mentioned right rudder to get us realigned with centerline and reduce the sideloading. The student used right rudder but accidentally had his foot on the brake as well as the rudder. This caused the plane to brake solely on the right side and begin skidding down the runway. Out of fear; I believe the brake was pushed slightly more as opposed to less. At this time I started calling that I had the flight controls and the student took his hands off of the controls. At this point; the aircraft was perpendicular to the runway. Momentum had the plane still rolling slowly. I was not sure at the time if there was any damage to the tires due to side load or skidding and did not want to apply brakes in an effort to reduce damage. At this point I treated the plane as if it was a soft field landing; I used minimal braking and let the plane come to a stop in the grass directly next to the runway. I have a very small feet and know for myself that if my heels are on the ground I am on the rudder. In order to touch the brake; my leg needs to be lifted. This is not the case for most other people. In the future; I have now learned that to reduce the chances of this happening again; I will verify on short final that the students have their feet only on the rudder and not touching the brakes. Instead of teaching 'heels on the ground' I will now specify that 'balls of feet should be on the rudders',,C-172 Instructor and Student pilot reported a runway excursion.
1829789,202108,,ZZZ.TRACON,US,155,10,,2000,,,Haze / Smoke; 7,,,3000,,TRACON ZZZ,FBO,DA40 Diamond Star,,2,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Cruise,None,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,TRACON ZZZ,,Mooney Aircraft Undifferentiated or Other Model,,1,Part 91,,,,,,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Total 960,,Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1829789,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence,Horizontal 350; Vertical 1000,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Weather; Human Factors; Procedure,Human Factors,Smokey day; still decent horizontal visibility but milky white sky. We were on flight following flying east and saw another traffic (not with flight following) on traffic system flying parallel to us on our left; also eastbound. We wanted to turn north; so we decided to make a right 270 degrees to the north in order to pass well behind that traffic. But just as we finished the turn; we realized traffic had turned right and was coming towards us. Out of the haze there appeared to be a Mooney like aircraft. It's bank; color; and convergence angle blended perfectly with the white haze. Even though traffic system said they were 500 feet above; it looked closer than that so I began a rapid descent and was soon clear of conflict. ZZZ was busy and didn't give the traffic alert until just before I saw them out of the haze. Conclusion: Be very careful of traffic during wildfire smoke; especially white aircraft on converging course; expect the unexpected when it comes to movement of other traffic; don't rely on ATC advisories.,,,,Instructor Pilot reported taking evasive action to avoid an aircraft that was obscured by weather.
1832934,202108,1801-2400,1W1.Airport,WA,,0.25,250,,,VMC,,,Night,,,CTAF 1W1,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Final Approach,,Class G ZSE,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Air Transport Pilot (ATP); Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 150; Flight Crew Total 20000; Flight Crew Type 1000,,Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification,,,1832934,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Object,,N,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Airport; Environment - Non Weather Related; Human Factors,Human Factors,Student and instructor were on a night cross-country. Traffic pattern was entered and to verify wind direction we did not descend on downwind but continued on an upwind leg to ensure we would be ready for the landing. We turned crosswind and downwind and did our before landing procedure. Student was slow to configure the aircraft which extended the downwind leg further than desired and upon turning base we noted we were low on the VASI. The student made a correction to get back on/above the glide path which was too little. I as the instructor was too late and too slow to inspire a more aggressive correction until the top of the tree came into view. I took control of the airplane and landed uneventfully and taxied to parking. There was no indication of flight control malfunction nor any indication of a loss of engine RPM. Subsequent inspection revealed slight damage to the right main landing gear fairing and damage to the left horizontal stabilizer fairing. I suspect that the propeller may have been impacted but there was no sudden stoppage of the prop. Of note; when the runway lights were activated by the CTAF; the lights on the north side of the runway from midfield to the departure end did not illuminate. What did come on was all of the lights on the south side of the runway and half the lights on the north side from the approach end to midfield. Also; I'm aware that the VASI glide slope angle is set higher than a three degree glide slope because of obstructions (trees) and the angle used to be published in the Chart Supplement; but that information is no longer available.,,,,Instructor reported possibly clipping a tree on approach due to being lower then normal.
1832946,202108,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,0,0,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO; Other Flight school,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Takeoff / Launch,,Class C ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 154; Flight Crew Total 4600; Flight Crew Type 92,,Training / Qualification; Workload,,,1832946,,,,,,,,,,,,Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Object; Ground Excursion Runway,,N,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Air Traffic Control Provided Assistance; Flight Crew Regained Aircraft Control; Flight Crew Returned To Gate,Human Factors,Human Factors,The following is my best recall of the events between approximately XA:00 and XB:30 Zulu on Date which resulted in damage to the aircraft.Student: Private Pilot seeking a Multi Engine add on ratingThe day's lesson was an introduction to engine failure procedures in the aircraft. We had previously covered these procedures in our simulator; most recently on date [two days prior]. Before the flight we reviewed the lesson plan; which was to include:1. I would conduct all communication with ATC during the flight so that he could focus on procedures.2. A simulated engine failure on takeoff to be verbalized by me as 'engine failure' with the student responding by retarding both throttles to idle and declaring an aborted takeoff. He did not respond to my first call; but on the second call of 'engine failure' he followed the procedure correctly.3. Simulated engine failure on climb out by retarding one throttle to idle and with the student following the appropriate response flow; then resetting the throttle for climb to the practice area. This went according to plan.4. Upon reaching maneuvering altitude in the practice area (4;000 feet) a simulated engine failure with fuel selector set to Off and the student following the response flow and troubleshooting checklist. This was followed by securing the engine per the checklist; then restarting per the checklist. This all went according to plan.5. Demonstration and practice of the VMC maneuver with engine failure simulated by throttle setting. This went according to plan.6. Return for landing; with simulated engine failure by throttle setting. This went according to plan.After landing; I requested a taxi back to the ramp as I thought the student was maxed out for the day based on previous flights and how much we had covered. However; as we had about 40 minutes left in our lesson block he asked if we could do some pattern work. Per his request I requested taxi instructions to Runway XXR. Once reaching the hold short line for [Runway] XXR I failed to recognize that the remaining flight was no as longer planned; and failed to develop and verbalize a brief specific to it. I was still operating under the assumption that we were practicing simulated engine failures per the original flight plan. In hindsight I believe that the student was operating under the assumption that we were setting up for pattern work with no planned (simulated) failures. We received clearance to take off and the student entered the runway following all normal procedures. He advanced the throttles for takeoff; and once we were rolling; but before positive airspeed indication; I retarded the right mixture control to idle cutoff (which we had done in the simulator on the previous lesson). The student did not respond to the engine failure; keeping both throttles full for take off. We immediately started veering south toward the right side of the runway. I called for the student to retard the throttles; but he did not respond. I moved the right mixture control full forward to restart the engine in an effort to eliminate the asymmetric thrust and regain directional control; but by then we were crossing the runway edge and about to run into a taxiway location sign (Taxiway 1). At this point the student did retard both throttles to idle. The nose wheel struck the location sign and the left propeller struck either a runway edge light or a taxiway light. We stopped on Taxiway 1; but in the process made a looping turn and ended up facing east on the taxiway. The Tower controller called to ask if we were alright and I responded that we were. I requested and received taxi instructions to our maintenance hangar. After clearing Runway XXL on the east side I provided more detail to the Tower controller and informed them that I would call with additional detail once I was back at the office; which I did. Additionally; Operations and Security personnel came to the office and took a statement from me. At this point the student had already left the school.Contributing factors:1. My failure to properly brief the unplanned scenario with the student and anticipate the potential failure.2. The student's failure to follow established procedure.3. No brakes on the right side limited my options for regaining control.,,,,Instructor pilot reported a student lost control of the aircraft during a simulated engine failure on departure.
1833492,202108,0601-1200,,,,,0,,,VMC,,,,12000,,,FBO,PA-28 Cherokee/Archer/Dakota/Pillan/Warrior,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,None,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Other Not at airport,Other not on aircraft,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 115; Flight Crew Total 568; Flight Crew Type 30,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1833492,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Single Pilot,Flight Crew Student,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 14; Flight Crew Total 14; Flight Crew Type 13,,Workload; Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness,,,1833494,Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence,,N,Person Flight Crew,Other Landing,General Flight Cancelled / Delayed,Human Factors,Human Factors,I received a phone call from a student saying that he had gone flying solo (which I was not informed on until after the flight. I tell all my students to text me before going to fly and once they are on the ground) and when he came in for a landing with a light crosswind coming from the right; he recognized he was slightly left of the centerline so he attempted to correct. After touchdown; due to the right crosswind; my student had left rudder in due to the sideslip situation for the crosswind; and the plane then pulled to the left. The plane then veered to the left and my student overcorrected with the right rudder resulting in him ending up in the grass. While the aircraft was moving in the grass off the right of the runway; my student attempts to stop in the grass and reports 'the aircraft pulled hard to the left causing me to cross back over the runway and coming to a rest on the left side of the runway'.This report is all [the] words from my student; as I was not at the airport due to me not knowing that the solo was happening. My student has submitted his own NASA report as well.,,I'm student pilot and I was doing a student solo. I started my flight with a take off on Runway XX and did some practice ground reference maneuvers south of ZZZ. After working ground reference maneuvers at about XA:50; I headed back to the airport to land for the day. I was on final for Runway XY and had a right crosswind; and was correcting with left rudder and right aileron. When about 10-15 feet off the runway; I was slightly left of center line and as soon as I touched down; my wheel was turned left because of the rudder so my plane was jerked slightly to the left; I attempted to use right rudder to straighten the aircraft and lost control and went off the right side of the runway. I then attempted to slow down my aircraft in the grass off the runway; but the aircraft pulled hard left causing me to cross the runway; coming to a rest on the left side of the runway. During the time that I was off the runway my engine had shut down. I then turned the keys off and pulled mixture all the way out and exited out of the aircraft.,,Student Pilot on a solo flight and the student's Flight Instructor reported a runway excursion occurred during crosswind landing.
1835114,202108,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,160,6,,2500,,VMC,,,Daylight,7000,,,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,3,Part 91,None,Training,,Cruise,,Class E ZZZ2,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Engine,,X,Failed; Malfunctioning,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 120; Flight Crew Total 817; Flight Crew Type 750,,Confusion; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Troubleshooting; Workload,,,1835114,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 60; Flight Crew Total 625; Flight Crew Type 300,,Situational Awareness; Workload; Troubleshooting; Time Pressure,,,1835159,Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence,,N,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Diverted; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action; Flight Crew Landed in Emergency Condition; General Evacuated,Weather; Human Factors; Aircraft,Human Factors,Familiarization flight with the airspace around ZZZ and carbureted C172 model with another instructor onboard. Departed ZZZ at approximately XA:00 local; After landing at ZZZ1; we departed southwest bound at 2;500'. I was flying the aircraft when we experienced a sudden loss of engine power; followed by complete engine loss. I gave controls to the other instructor and began troubleshooting / running checklists - Checked fuel selector / gauges; mixture/throttle; carb heat; and were unable to get it restarted. We turned south for a cornfield and began preparing for an off field landing while I contacted ZZZ Tower to let them know of our situation. The other instructor onboard maneuvered for a safe landing on the cornfield. Once the aircraft was secured; we exited the plane and inspected everything. No injuries or damage to the aircraft / property. I called Clearance Delivery and asked them to let ZZZ Tower know that we were okay. I spoke with various agencies over the next 30 minutes. I let them know we were okay and the plane was undamaged. We shared our location with flight school management; who then drove out and brought extra fuel. We began straining fuel; which all came back clean. Then added approx 5 gallons to each fuel tanks and did a thorough run up on the engine - All gauges were green and no issues seen. After discussing we came to the conclusion of carburetor icing affecting engine performance. We were at a relatively low cruise setting with high humidity due to showers/storms in the area. When troubleshooting in the air earlier; pulling the carb heat had no affect on engine RPM. We commenced a soft/short field takeoff from the cornfield and landed safely back at ZZZ.,,Loss of RPM; suspected Carb icing. Insufficient power. Ran checklist; restart and shutdown checklist. No damage to aircraft or landing site. No injury.,,Three Instructor Pilots reported an engine failure while on a familiarization flight in a single engine aircraft. The PF landed off airport in a nearby field. It was later determined the engine probably failed due to carburetor icing.
1835471,202108,1201-1800,ZZZ.Tower,US,300,2.5,700,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Final Approach,Visual Approach; STAR ZZZZZ,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ZZZ,,Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng,,2,,,,,Initial Approach; Final Approach,,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Instrument; Other CFII,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 12; Flight Crew Total 730; Flight Crew Type 550,,Workload; Communication Breakdown; Troubleshooting; Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Confusion,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1835471,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance,Horizontal 500; Vertical 250,N,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Air Traffic Control Separated Traffic; Flight Crew Requested ATC Assistance / Clarification; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,We were coming back to ZZZ (our base) from ZZZ1. We were assigned ZZZZZ Arrival. Shortly after crossing the shoreline; Tower told us to maneuver toward a landmark to follow the traffic. After we made our turn; Tower asked us to if we have the light transport traffic in sight; my student pointed out a traffic to me and I radioed the tower that I had the traffic in sight. Tower then told us to cross behind the light transport traffic and cleared us for Runway XXL. After the traffic my student pointed out passed in front of us we angled toward the base leg. then I realized that traffic is not a light transport. Then I inspected the final for Runway XXR and saw a light transport about 250 ft. below; and about 500 ft. north east of us. I took over the airplane and maneuvered to avoid flying in front of the light transport. [The] maneuver was successful and we flew behind them. Shortly after the evasive maneuver Tower asked us again if we have the light transport traffic in sight; I told them 'We do have [light transport] in sight' We proceeded to land on Runway XXL.In retrospect; I shouldn't have told the tower we have the traffic in sight without positively identifying the light transport. A good radio transmission  would be 'we do have a traffic over X location please confirm that is our traffic.',,,,Flight Instructor reported a NMAC in the traffic pattern. The Instructor and student misidentified the aircraft they were to follow per ATC. The Instructor took control and maneuvered the aircraft into the correct traffic pattern flow.
1837876,202109,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,0,0,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,UNICOM ZZZ,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,2,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Taxi; Landing,,Class G ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,UNICOM ZZZ,,Cardinal 177/177RG,,,Part 91,VFR,,,Landing,,Class G ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 257; Flight Crew Total 1692; Flight Crew Type 490,,Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1837876,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical,,,Person Flight Crew,Taxi,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,We were doing traffic pattern operations and Aircraft Y joined the pattern. Due to the runway being short we were doing land and taxi backs. On our second to last landing we were taxing back to the taxi via the runway. During this time Aircraft Y called short final. I took controls from my student and expedited the taxi. We cleared the runway with only about 5 seconds before touchdown. Aircraft Y cleared the runway behind us and departed shortly after us. As we were in downwind Aircraft Y said that he was number two following the Aircraft X. As we landed we heard him calls for a final again. When we turned around to back taxi Aircraft Y was already in his round out to flare. I directed the student to get to the right side of the runway. This gave us the most room from Aircraft Y since he was not going to go around and we did not have a safe place to clear the runway. As he can just stop he turned off the runway and got in front of us to taxi back to the hanger.During this incursion I believe the main cause was decision making process. Even though the runway is 200 ft wide there should not be two airplanes on the runway. I believe Aircraft Y thought that with that being 200 ft wide that he'll be okay landing at the same time we were taxiing back. He also did not use his radio to tell us what his plans were.,,,,A Flight Instructor conducting training at a non-towered airport reported they back taxied on the runway after landing two times causing a near collision with a trailing aircraft which was landing and had reported on final approach behind them.
1837924,202109,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,,1500,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Climb; Descent,,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Air Taxi,Small Transport,,1,Part 135,,Passenger,,Cruise,,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Air Transport Pilot (ATP); Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 40; Flight Crew Total 15000; Flight Crew Type 2000,,Workload; Distraction; Confusion,,,1837924,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC,Vertical 250,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors; Airspace Structure,Human Factors,I departed ZZZ; informing the Tower Controller that I would be doing flight training over [the city] at 3500 ft. and below and that I would remain on his frequency. He also advised Aircraft Y; Aircraft Y on my ADS-B; of our presence and altitude -1;000 ft. - and the pilot said he had us in sight. I was watching him on my iPad using ForeFlight. When the traffic was called; I was concluding the engine-out glide; as the student had successfully put the aircraft in a position to land on the grass strip. At 1;000 ft.; I had the student initiate a climb and had him turn away from the path of Aircraft Y. As we climbed to 1;200 feet; Aircraft Y turned to cross over us. 1838420,202109,1201-1800,SBA.TRACON,CA,286,5,,6000,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,TRACON SBA,FBO,Small Aircraft,,2,Part 91,IFR,Training,,Cruise,Direct,Class E ZLA,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Small Aircraft,,,,,,,,Direct,Class E ZLA,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 49; Flight Crew Total 306; Flight Crew Type 269,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1838420,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Airborne Conflict; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 3000; Vertical 300,N,Person Air Traffic Control; Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Air Traffic Control Provided Assistance; Air Traffic Control Issued Advisory / Alert; Flight Crew Returned To Clearance; Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,On an Instrument cross-country from ZZZ to SMX; we had just finished a descent from 8;000 ft. to 6;000ft. at ATC's direction as we passed over top of the RZS VOR. We were advised of traffic 12 o'clock; opposite direction. I can't recall if ATC said they were talking to the other aircraft or not; but we advised ATC that we were searching. We saw the other aircraft come up on our transponder at 500 ft. below and climbing; and I tagged the aircraft to monitor while continuing a visual scan. Once the aircraft got within 6nm; I instructed the student to remove his VLDs (View Limiting Device) and look for the traffic as well since the target had now moved to within 300 ft. and still indicating a climb on ADS-B.Approximately the time that the traffic target got within a 2 mile range; I finally saw the aircraft come into view. Their paint scheme was grey with blue; and made it hard to distinguish them against the mountainous terrain. They were exactly 12 o'clock and slightly low; maybe 200-300 ft. I took controls and initiated an evasive steep turn to the right; in accordance with 91.113. At roughly the same time; ATC called us to initiate another traffic advisory for traffic less than 2 miles. We replied that we had the traffic in sight and were deviating to avoid them. ATC then instructed to maintain visual separation; and we re-intercepted our course once we were well clear. My student said they were close enough to see the people in the other cockpit; and both of us felt that the encounter was way too close for comfort. The other aircraft did not appear to alter course to avoid our aircraft.I believe contributing factors may have been that the other pilot may not have been in contact with ATC; and that they were not flying a standard VFR/IFR altitude or were possibly using an inappropriate altimeter setting for their location. In the future; I will advise ATC that traffic is not in-sight sooner so that ATC can issue a vector to ensure adequate spacing.,,,,Flight Instructor reported an airborne conflict occurred during cruise flight with another aircraft. Reportedly; the other aircraft was not in communication with ATC or flying a standard altitude for their direction of flight.
1838447,202109,1801-2400,ZZZ.TRACON,US,,0,,1900,,VMC,10,,Daylight,9000,,CTAF ZZZ,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Initial Approach,Visual Approach,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 200; Flight Crew Total 600,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Other,,1838447,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Vertical 150,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors; Procedure,Human Factors,Student Training Flight; Transitioned through ZZZ airspace from North to South towards ZZZ1. ATC at ZZZ was advised of Aircraft X (our aircraft) of the destination. Parachute operations were occurring at the airport. Pilot flying was able to contact advisory frequency early due to a request made to the ATC at ZZZ. Pilot made incoming calls to overfly the field and enter left downwind Runway XX at approx. 5 and 3 miles and while over the runway. Helicopter making right traffic in pattern turning crosswind. Parachute operations made call while Aircraft X was over the airport of a 2 minute warning of parachuting operations being made by skydiving plane. Skydiver was approximately missed by 125 above at 1;900 feet MSL or 1;500 feet AGL. Aircraft X was inbound to make a tear drop entry into left downwind [Runway] XX. Pilots of jump plane were in contact with ZZZ Approach.Prevention: Parachute operating facilities need to be more aware of regulations105.23(c) A parachutist may drift over that airport with a fully deployed and properly functioning parachute if the parachutist is at least 2;000 feet above that airport's traffic pattern; and avoids creating a hazard to air traffic or to persons and property on the ground.If traffic is in the pattern or coming into the pattern and overflying the field and prior acknowledgment is made. Parachute operations need to hold passengers for release until Air Traffic has cleared and no longer are Hazards.In addition; Pilots transitioning from South out of ZZZ could be advised if parachute operations are about to occur; I.E. at time at which the parachutes are dropping and when the Area is clear again. The displacement between ZZZ airspace and ZZZ1 is merely 1 mile. This is not adequate time to change to Unicom and advised traffic of being inbound; Unless the pilot is able to change frequency early and make appropriate calls.,,,,Flight Instructor reported a near miss with a parachutist over the airport.

While conducting a simulated engine failure single-engine ILS approach to Runway XX at ZZZ; ATC; (i.e.; ZZZ Approach Control); vectored the applicant onto final. Once laterally established on the approach; ATC switched the applicant over to the common traffic advisory frequency. ATC provided no further traffic advisories or alertsThe applicant then switched to the advisory frequency and announced his position as a five (5) mile final to Runway XX. Aircraft Y then announced downwind for Runway XY. I then told the applicant that in the event of go-around; both engines were available. The applicant continued while I searched for traffic in haze and seven mile visibility. The applicant reported a three (3) mile final. I continued to scan for Aircraft Y. I told the applicant that I had not spotted the traffic and then radioed that we were on a one and one-half (1 and ½) mile final. In response; Aircraft Y stated they had us in sight. I asked them to go-around. Instead; they called they were turning final for Runway XY. When the applicant called one hundred feet (100') above minimums; I spotted Aircraft Y. At that time; I told the applicant the runway was in sight and the applicant removed his foggles. I pointed the traffic to the applicant at one to two o'clock and less than a quarter (1/4) mile and again asked Aircraft Y to execute a go-around; which he then did as he flew over the top of us at the intersection of Runway XX and Runway XY. As the applicant flared to land; the tail struck the pavement. Only then did I realize that the applicant failed to complete the before landing checklist; by extending the gear; which I; in turn; failed to observe.,,On Date I was taking a multi-engine commercial check ride with Designated Pilot Examiner [DPE] Name. I was the pilot in command for the flight. After flying the maneuvers we set up for the ILS XX into ZZZ. We had a simulated engine failure during the approach. ZZZ approach approved frequency change and gave no traffic advisories. I made a 5 mile final call on the CTAF followed by a 3 mile final call. During a 2 mile final Aircraft Y made a final call for Runway XY. I still had the foggles on and the [DPE] was searching for the traffic. I announced we reached the DA; and at that time name told me to remove the foggles. He was still searching for the traffic and talking to the other aircraft. Aircraft Y announced they would go around and I continued my approach inbound for Runway XX. With all the confusion and concerns of a mid-air collision i failed to complete the before landing check. It wasn't realized that the gear was retracted until the tail struck.Distraction and pressure were two major human factors that contributed to this incident. The other aircraft distracted me from completing the before landing check. In addition; the pressure of flying the approach and completing the maneuver within standards played a role.,,Flight crew reported distractions from a near mid air collision resulted in the landing check list not being performed and a gear up landing.
1839373,202108,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,347,1,,1900,,,30,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Other Downwind,None,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Initial Approach,Visual Approach,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 97; Flight Crew Total 700; Flight Crew Type 664,,Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1839373,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance,Horizontal 200; Vertical 100,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,As my private students and I returned from a local practice area; we were told to enter midfield right downwind for Runway XX. We were approximately 8 miles west of ZZZ at this point. Continuing inbound; we heard several other people coming back into ZZZ from practice areas and some other transient traffic. Just before we turned onto downwind at 1900 MSL; I looked up and to the right to saw an Aircraft Y also flying on downwind above me. When I turned downwind; I could no longer see him; as he was 6 o'clock high. At 2;400' MSL; Aircraft Y reported having us in sight and tower clear them to land as they are flying over top of us.  I noticed on the MFD that their ADS-B target had resulted in a traffic alert that was getting closer and descending. I pushed the nose forward and checked in with Tower abeam the numbers. The traffic passed over us very close. Seeing +02 on the MFD for the traffic; I initiated a left turn just as tower was instructing a left 360. I noted 1600 MSL on the altimeter; so I had descended 300' from traffic pattern altitude to evade the Aircraft Y. On final; I heard the Aircraft Y tell tower; 'we were extremely close to that downwind traffic on base.' Tower responded with; 'well he said he had you in sight; and Roanoke vectored you in that way; so I don't know what else to say about that.' We performed our touch and go and final lap before making a full stop. Bottom line; the Aircraft Y was overtaking me from the rear; told Tower he had me in sight; and was then cleared to land. I took evasive action; and even so; the traffic got within a few hundred feet of our aircraft. If we had not had ADS-B in; they might have hit us as they descended through Traffic Pattern Altitude.,,,,Flight Instructor reported an NMAC event during landing pattern training. Instructor initiated an evasive maneuver to avoid a collision.
1839623,202109,1201-1800,ZZZ.ARTCC,US,,0,300,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,10000,,CTAF ZZZ,Other school,Helicopter,,1,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,Visual Approach,Class G ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Part 91,,,,Initial Climb,,Class G ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Air Traffic Control Fully Certified; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument,Air Traffic Control Military 2; Flight Crew Last 90 Days 350; Flight Crew Total 1500; Flight Crew Type 400,,Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload; Other / Unknown; Communication Breakdown; Confusion,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1839623,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway,Horizontal 500; Vertical 100,N,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,My student and I entered the pattern at ZZZ from the NE. Upon checking in we heard one other aircraft in the pattern doing touch and goes. My student was flying and I was coordinating with the other aircraft on the radio. As my student and I entered 45 degree to left base [Runway] XY we could not get a visual on the the other aircraft that was on final XY. I instructed my student to perform a left 270 for separation. When we rejoined left base XY and gained visual on the other aircraft which was now on the go [Runway] XY. We called final XY and chose to shoot the landing to XY at intersection 1. At 100 feet AGL I noticed a landing light slightly below our altitude coming from the opposite direction. I took immediate control of the aircraft and performed a descending left turn to avoid the oncoming aircraft. We landed on taxiway 2 just north of taxiway 3. I successfully hailed the plane departing Runway XZ which informed me they 'had made an on the go call' and that they 'had a visual on us the entire time'. They made a call 'departing to the Northwest' and that was their last call on frequency. At no point did the aircraft departing RWY XZ take evasive actions.I contacted the CFI in the other plane that had performed the touch and go on Runway XY ahead of us and he confirmed he had not heard the aircraft departing XZ make any radio calls.,,,,Helicopter Pilot reported a NMAC with an opposite direction aircraft at a non-towered airport. The opposite direction aircraft did not take any evasive action and did not announce; on CTAF; its intentions or position.

1840712,202109,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,CTAF ZZZ,Personal,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,1,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Landing,Direct,Class G ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Hangar / Base,,FBO,Other / Unknown; Supervisor of Flying,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,,,Human-Machine Interface; Other / Unknown; Training / Qualification,,,1840712,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway,,,Person Flight Crew,Other Landing,,Human Factors,Human Factors,I was performing the duties of the Supervisor for the afternoon shift (XA:00-XF:00). I reviewed and endorsed a student pilots flight planning to do a solo cross country from ZZZ-ZZZ1-ZZZ. I found the flight planning accurate and correct and so went forward endorsing the student to make the flight. The weather for the day was VFR and well within his PQ card limitations with the only major concern being a crosswind of approximately 6 knots (his max x-wind was 8 kts). Also; prior to letting him make the flight I just expressed to him if the clouds were by chance going to drop to immediately come back to the field because clouds in the local practice areas had been reported at various heights around 4;000 feet MSL. Other than that I saw no issue with the student pilot making the flight to ZZZ1. However; after maybe 45 mins after the students departure I received a call on the cell phone from the student saying that in the process of landing he had gone off the side of the runway and was in the grass. I immediately informed someone up the chain of command who then helped getting the correct people to help and develop a plan of action and try to learn what exactly happened. With the help of the Flight Ops; Chief Pilot; and maintenance personnel; we learned that the student had possibly porpoised upon landing which resulted in the aircraft going off the runway and experiencing damage. A rescue crew including one maintenance pilot and the student pilot's instructor flew down to ZZZ1 to assess the situation and bring the student pilot back to ZZZ.,,,,Supervisor of collegiate flight program reported student on solo cross country experienced a runway excursion. Supervisor dispatched a crew to assess the situation and retrieve the student.
1841397,202109,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,1,,1600,,VMC,6,,Daylight,22000,,Tower ZZZ,,PA-28 Cherokee/Archer/Dakota/Pillan/Warrior,,,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Other Traffic Pattern,None,Class D GFK,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ZZZ,,PA-28 Cherokee/Archer/Dakota/Pillan/Warrior,,,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Climb,,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Not Flying; Instructor,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 30; Flight Crew Total 257; Flight Crew Type 225,,Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Confusion; Distraction,,,1841397,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Trainee; Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Private,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 5; Flight Crew Total 130; Flight Crew Type 5,,Situational Awareness; Distraction; Confusion; Workload; Training / Qualification,,,1841375,ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence,Horizontal 2500; Vertical 0,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Procedure; Human Factors,Human Factors,While flying with a student on a student pilot lesson we made evasive action to avoid a conflict. I am the Flight Instructor and immediately took flight controls and made the evasive actions to avoid traffic in Class D airspace. The situation Aircraft X was on UPWIND in the traffic pattern climbing to TPA (traffic pattern altitude) and turning Crosswind. I was in Aircraft Y squaring our turn to enter a downwind at TPA. Aircraft Z was following me into the traffic pattern to come into land. Tower told us at a visual checkpoint to fly west and square our turn to enter a downwind (north) for the traffic pattern. We had a strong left quartering headwind pushing us north toward the pattern. Aircraft X was out of sight underneath the cowling. Tower asked if we had traffic (Aircraft X) in sight ahead. We did not. Student flying drifting into the pattern and slowly correcting. After Traffic came into sight it was closer than I feel was comfortable less than .5 mile. We were drifting at TPA north and toward traffic; Aircraft X was climbing and turning toward us. As Aircraft X became visual ADS-B made a 'TRAFFIC SAME ALTITUDE 12 O'CLOCK' call. I took flight controls and banked left to avoid traffic to fly south. As I was turning south Aircraft Z was getting closer to us. I stopped my turn at 160-170 and banked a slight turn right to allow Aircraft Z to pass us.The problem arose because of lack of wind correction angle; ATC call; and traffic separation. Contributing factors strong low altitude winds; high traffic congestion; lack of traffic in sight. Corrective actions were speaking about wind correction angle after landing; drawing the situation; ATC workload; the ability to say UNABLE then adjusting flight for safety of flight. Human performance considerations decision of me to allow the student to drift off course and not correct faster. ATC high workload with Aircraft zooming into land. My student and I debriefed after we landed about how we could have avoided the problem and how we will do better next time on our flight. It was a good teaching moment for high workload areas; ATC clearances; and safety of flight.,,For context; I am a student. I am currently transitioning from a C172 over to a Piper. While doing pattern work at ZZZ; a close call occurred during the upwind leg of the pattern. I pushed the Piper's nose down a little to clear my crosswind turn; and began to make the turn. A few seconds later I saw another one of the [FBO] aircraft; at the same altitude; not moving. I realized our aircraft were on a collision course and took immediate evasive action to avoid the oncoming aircraft. About the same time I was taking Evasive actions my CFI saw the traffic on ADS-B. Tower was not calling our crosswind and no alarms in the aircraft sounded. It is unclear if the other aircraft took evasive actions as well. The issue was resolved by rejoining the downwind and resuming normal operations.It is also unknown if Tower was aware of the other aircraft's position. I feel that if Tower had called our base; the situation would have been avoided completely. Overall this really shook me up. I regathered myself and finished the lesson; but both me and my CFI were upset with the controller and rattled by the situation. Seeing the growing silhouette of another airplane; unmoving and hanging in the air is a terrifying thing to experience; and I hope that less pilots have to go through it.,,An instructor pilot and student reported an NMAC while taking evasive action to avoid two other aircraft in the pattern.
1841921,202109,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,,,,VMC,6,,Daylight,CLR,,CTAF ZZZ,Personal,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,1,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Takeoff / Launch,Visual Approach,Class G ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer,,,,,,,Taxi,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying; Single Pilot,Flight Crew Student,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 10.3; Flight Crew Total 53.1,,Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Situational Awareness,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1841921,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 1200; Vertical 750,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,I am a student pilot who had an incident this morning at ZZZ. I was flying solo and preparing to takeoff. I taxied behind the hold-short line while two aircraft landed in succession. After watching the second aircraft land and move down the runway (approximately three minutes); I radioed my takeoff intentions; rolled into position on the Runway (XX) and scanned for the aircraft that had just landed. I watched it in distance continue to move down to the end of the runway. I was unaware the aircraft had to taxi-back and began my takeoff. When I spotted the aircraft taxiing back (approximately 1;200 feet horizontal) I began lift off and maneuvered to the right of the runway. As I passed by the aircraft from the air; it was not on the runway; but crossing from the runway to the taxiway. I was approximately 750 feet above the runway.I should have waited longer but it was difficult to see the aircraft at the other end of the runway and I assumed they had exited the runway; but hadn't radioed their new position. I also should have known they had to taxi back and the time I waited for them to clear probably did more harm than good.,,,,C172 student pilot reported taking off while an aircraft was back taxiing on the same runway at a non-towered airport. 1842590,202109,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,CTAF ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Air Transport Pilot (ATP); Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 60; Flight Crew Total 10350; Flight Crew Type 800,,Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification,,,1842590,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway,,,,,Aircraft Aircraft Damaged; Flight Crew Regained Aircraft Control; General Maintenance Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,During flight training; the student pilot flared aggressively resulting in the airplane being 4 or 5 ft. above the Runway at low speed with flaps fully extended. I told the student to go around. He delayed but added full power after a second or two. He then raised the nose abruptly resulting in an immediate stall warning. I attempted to lower the nose but the student remained on the controls and continued to pull back. As a result; I was unable to reduce the angle of attack. The airplane stalled and began to roll and yaw to the left. The airplane was only a few ft. above the Runway. The student released the controls but the aircraft was stalled and had no control effectiveness. I reduce the thrust to idle to arrest the incipient spin and the airplane landed on the left main landing gear. It was not a hard landing but the airplane continued to roll to the left. The left wingtip contacted the Runway surface. We were then at about a 45 degree angle to the Runway Centerline and exited the Runway into the grass. I regained directional control and brought the airplane to a stop.There were no injuries. As of this writing; the only damage I am aware of is a cracked and broken plastic wing tip and some slightly bent aluminum at the left wing tip. Mechanics are inspecting the airplane now.,,,,C172 Flight Instructor reported student improperly attempted landing; lost control; which resulted in runway excursion and aircraft damage.
1844445,202110,1201-1800,UES.Airport,WI,,3,,2000,,Mixed,10,,,1300,,Tower UES,FBO,PA-28 Cherokee/Archer/Dakota/Pillan/Warrior,,2,Part 91,IFR,Training,,Final Approach,Vectors,Class D UES,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,GPS & Other Satellite Navigation,,X,Malfunctioning,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 50; Flight Crew Total 270; Flight Crew Type 270,,Confusion; Troubleshooting; Distraction; Situational Awareness,,,1844445,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation - Altitude Undershoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,General None Reported / Taken,Human Factors; Software and Automation,Human Factors,Vectored to ILS/LOC 10 into UES; had base of clouds around 2;300 AGL; the at or above altitude for our final approach fix. I entered flight plan into top Garmin unit and had user error. I was expecting G430's to be in cooperation with one another after entering flight plan and programming. In the moment forgetting this morning we encountered an updating information error in one of our G430's. While being vectored; I spent too much time trying to problem solve why my G430's weren't in unison rather than paying attention to my altitude. 1844625,202110,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,Rain; 7,,Daylight,11000,,Tower ZZZ,Other school,PA-28 Cherokee/Archer/Dakota/Pillan/Warrior,,2,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Takeoff / Launch,None,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Multiengine; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 73.6; Flight Crew Total 332.6; Flight Crew Type 303,,Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness,,,1844625,,,,,,,,,,,,Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Aircraft Aircraft Damaged,Human Factors,Human Factors,On Date; we experienced a runway excursion event at ZZZ. I was the CFI on board and I was providing flight training to a student pilot working towards their private pilot certificate. The excursion occurred on our initial takeoff out of the airport. The student pilot was initially on the controls and we were attempting a soft field takeoff on Runway XXR which is 3;XXX feet long by XX feet wide. Everything was normal up until we began to rotate which was around 40 kts. Upon rotation; we had too much aft elevator pressure causing our nose to pitch up to around 16 degrees. Along with this high pitch; too much right rudder input was made causing a yaw and roll to the right. We departed the right side of the runway and then we reduced the power to idle and slowed down in a straight line. There were no injuries and only minor damage to the propeller and skidplate. A few notable factors that I think attributed to this incident are as follows: The excessive pitch up reduced our visibility over the cowling and prevented us from noticing the extent to which we were drifting off to the right. The reduction of left wind correction during the takeoff roll. And the application of too much right rudder causing a further drift to the right. As for corrective action to prevent similar situations in the future: As a CFI I could improve my defensive positioning in a way to prevent excessive pitch and rudder inputs. I can set more strict personal standards in when to take over flight controls as well as making sure to be more distinctive in taking controls. And I can improve my ground instruction by providing more distinct visual references for students to look for when making control inputs. Overall; this was an unfortunate situation but I do look forward to learning from this mistake and helping to ensure others don't fall into the same situation.,,,,PA-28 Flight Instructor reported excessive pitch up and right rudder input by the student resulted in a runway excursion during takeoff.

Aircraft Y was a Cherokee (I think). My student and I had been flying VFR patterns at ZZZ for approximately 30 minutes; making all our normal calls on CTAF even though we were the only aircraft in the pattern the entire time. Due to winds and sun angle we were utilizing Runway XX. Upon our missed approach from the fifth pattern; while on the upwind still climbing out; we observed Aircraft Y on a collision course with us. That aircraft was approaching the airport straight-in to Runway YY. There had been NO position calls from that aircraft up to that point. I immediately initiated evasive action and passed approximately 1;000 feet to the right (due to the angles at the time) and nearly co-altitude with the aircraft. Only after I queried the aircraft did he respond and confirm his tail number. He maintained a too-close position to us even though we were reporting our position to him relative to his airplane as well as our position in the pattern. This individual maintained that he had made requisite position calls; but he had clearly not and likely not even been on the frequency. He apparently did not understand/hear that we were working the opposing runway...or he didn't care.We departed the pattern after the pattern following the conflict. Aircraft Y landed full stop.,,,,DA-40 Flight Instructor reported an NMAC during climbout with another aircraft approaching the opposite end of the same runway; requiring evasive action. Reportedly; the pilot of the other aircraft had not made any position announcements.

Contact was made with center after being handed off by Departure and the instrument approach was executed with a touch and go on Runway XX. After the touch and go the Instructor and Student were startled by a TCAS/ Terrain warning which led to a deviation from the missed approach procedure. Once contact was re-established with Center the student and instructor were called out for a possible pilot deviation and given the number to call. While the instructor failed to remind the student of their responsibility as instrument pilots to execute the missed approach on an IFR flight plan; due to the Terrain warning both pilots decided to alter course to maintain obstruction and terrain clearance which led to the deviation. Both pilots will be calling the number and starting the recovery process asap; as well as completing FAA online IFR recurring courses.,,With an instructor on board; I filed an IFR cross-country flight plan to ZZZ via ZZZ ZZZ1 ZZZ with the RNAV Y into ZZZ1 for a touch-and-go (as stated in the flight plan remarks). After the touch-and-go; both my instructor and I were startled by a TCAS/Terrain warning which led to a deviation from the missed approach procedure as we turned from the surrounding hills. Once contact was re-established with Center; we were called out for a possible pilot deviation and given a number to call. While the instructor failed to remind the student of their responsibility as instrument pilots to execute the missed approach on an IFR flight plan; due to the Terrain warning both pilots decided to alter course to maintain obstruction and terrain clearance which led to the deviation. 1847286,202110,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,Turbulence; 10,,Daylight,10000,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Light Sport Aircraft,,1,Part 91,VFR,Training,,Landing,Direct,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Pilot Flying; Single Pilot,Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Private,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 19.4; Flight Crew Total 159.4; Flight Crew Type 159.4,,Situational Awareness,,,1847286,,,,,,,,,,,,Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Aircraft Aircraft Damaged,Aircraft; Human Factors; Weather,Human Factors,The PIAT is a small lightweight aircraft. When landing at Runway XX at ZZZ the front tire blew. The aircraft had landed on the runway and looked as if everything was normal but then the aircraft became airborne again. This could've been due to a gust of wind that lifted the aircraft. It could've been the fact that Runway XX starts off as a flat runway and then slopes downward. Either way if you are in an aircraft that likes to glide recognize the risk for becoming airborne again. It didn't take much to blow the front tire; I was airborne for maybe 1/2 a second or less and then made contact with the runway again. The PIAT aircraft does not have individual brakes on the main tires (unlike a Cessna 172); it has one brake lever that operates the brakes in unison. If for some reason your nose wheel blows you should anticipate uncontrollable turn. I used full right rudder and applied full brakes to avoid going off the runway; but we still drifted left. At the same time of sliding down the runway I shut off mags to stop the propeller from spinning (minimizing risk and moving parts). I did this because I knew that the nose was low to the ground thus making the ground clearance on the propeller low. This all happened within 1/2 a second; meaning time to go-around was not an option. If you are in an aircraft that is a natural glider be careful on landings not to become airborne again. If you do become airborne again and can recognize it fast going around would be your best choice.,,,,PIAT (Light Sport Aircraft) pilot reported the aircraft became airborne for 1/2 a second after touchdown due to possible gusts resulting in a blown front tire; loss of aircraft control; and a near runway excursion.
1848580,202107,1201-1800,IND.Airport,IN,,,0,,,,,,,,,Ground IND,FBO,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,,Training,,Taxi,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Ground IND,FBO,Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer,,2,Part 91,IFR,Training,,Taxi,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Flight Instructor,,,Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Confusion,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1848580,,,,,,,,,,,,ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical,,,Person Flight Crew,Taxi,Flight Crew Requested ATC Assistance / Clarification,Human Factors,Human Factors,Approximately XA00; the student [Aircraft X] was taxiing to depart IND while the instructor was monitoring. We were given instructions to taxi to 23L via M; M3; cross 32; N; and to hold short of D. While approaching 32 ground was coordinating with an Aircraft Y plane on D just short of N trying to return to ramp; and Aircraft Z (air carrier) plane on 14 trying to get to point X. Initially; ground control told the Aircraft Y plane to hold short so the Aircraft Z could turn right onto D then left into point 2; but Aircraft Z crew offered to continue down 14 and enter the ramp at point 1 which is essentially where our taxi route was. Ground hesitated then approved this request just about when we were crossing the hold short lines to cross 32. We noticed Aircraft Z began speeding up their taxi and the student noted hesitation whether to continue further onto the runway. Since we had already begun crossing the hold short lines I instructed her to continue but to expedite taxi. At this point; Aircraft Z was still just past D with what I had thought would be plenty of forward visibility to see us crossing directly in front of them. As we pulled onto N I became concerned Aircraft Z may not see us as the amount of thrust he was using and my perceived distance he was behind us indicated to me he was expediting his taxi into the ramp. As we approached our hold short instruction at D I radioed ground to confirm Aircraft Z had us in sight. At this point; I don't even think Aircraft Z was still on ground frequency even though he was still on N which is what I was hoping for to give him notice of our position if he was unaware. Before ground responded Aircraft Z began their turn into their ramp at point 2 off N as we came to a stop holding short of D. I was having a hard time judging how far they were behind us due to lack of rearward visibility; and was close to increasing throttle and continuing on delta without clearance but did not. It is hard to tell; but as Aircraft Z turned it seemed to me and the student their right wing crossed over our horizontal stabilizer or at least very close to it. This is what in hindsight seemed to confirm my suspicions they never saw us. After a short delay as we were holding short ground responded something to the effect of; 'Um; Aircraft X yeah the Aircraft Z is clear of Delta so you can continue taxi Delta to 23L.' This indicated to me he did not really understand what I was communicating and was likely unaware of the hazard that had just occurred.In hindsight; I could have cued up ground a little sooner as to my concerns. I wrongly assumed the Aircraft Z saw us. I also should have simply taken control and taxied onto D without clearance and immediately notified ATC as there was no conflict on D. It is entirely possible the Aircraft Y did see us; and spacing was fine - hard to tell with limitations in rearward visibility; but either way it made both instructor and student extremely uncomfortable. If Aircraft Z did not see us I believe there is some responsibility on their shoulders of seeing traffic as we were off their nose at least 1;500 feet ahead of them when they accepted altered taxi instructions; and I believe they deviated from their taxi routing as they were cleared to point 1 but followed us on N to enter at point 2 creating the hazard. Also; ground control seemed unaware of the possible conflict giving Aircraft Z a taxi route without confirming our position along our route and without confirming Aircraft Z had us in sight. I'm also not sure whether they landed on 14; or if it was coming out of maintenance and they were taxing to ramp. I would think the latter as I think I'd have seen them land if so as a 14 landing would be unusual for the winds and traffic.The instructor should have been more proactive in contacting ground earlier upon possible conflict; and should have deviated per PIC authority from clearance to be 100% safety of flight was not compromised. Aircraft Z should be more aware of potential for not identifying small aircraft on taxi; and deviated from their ATC taxi clearance creating a hazard. Ground control should not accept taxi routing suggestions from pilots without being 100% certain they do not create a hazard; and confirming all prior traffic will not be at risk. Ground should have confirmed Aircraft Z had us in sight if they were going to be closely following our routing. I do think it would be pertinent to notify ATC of this event for them to play back and learn from this as well.,,,,Small Aircraft Flight Instructor reported that during taxi the wing of a transport category aircraft may have passed over the horizontal stabilizer of the smaller instructional aircraft. Reporter stated that IND Ground Control did not notify the large aircraft of the position of the small aircraft.

1849117,202110,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,0,,,VMC,10,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Landing,Visual Approach,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Rudder Pedal,,X,Improperly Operated,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 130; Flight Crew Total 1600; Flight Crew Type 1450,,Communication Breakdown; Training / Qualification; Time Pressure,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1849117,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Regained Aircraft Control; General Flight Cancelled / Delayed,Human Factors,Human Factors,My student and I were doing touch and goes at ZZZ; on departure on the crosswind to downwind leg at approximately 1;000 feet AGL; I reduced the power to idle and simulated an engine failure. I told my student to make a power off landing and make it a full stop. He glided the aircraft back to the runway and landed normally. Immediately after landing my student started to lose directional control of the aircraft and started to oscillate on the rudder pedals. I then instructed my student to regain control by applying equal and consistent pressure on the rudder pedals; I was also on the pedals assisting him. We started to approach the halfway point on the runway and I told my student he needed to start braking. He then pulled on the handbrake excessively hard which caused the wheels to lock up. While the wheels were locked up; he proceeded to start oscillating again with the rudder pedals. I took controls and audibly told him 'my controls'. When I pushed on the handbrake forward to release the brakes; he bumped into the throttle and advanced it; at this point we started to accelerate towards the end of the runway; I immediately pulled the throttle back; regained directional control and applied the brakes consistently/smoothly. I was able to safely exit the runway at the last taxiway. After this incident; I had a meeting with the owner of the flight school and we decided to drop this student from the program. This was not the first 'incident' with this student. He had flown previously with the assistant chief pilot and other senior instructors; after they hit a 'wall' with him in training and he was no longer progressing; I took over. Of the approximately 6 flights I had with this student; 3 had 'incidents' where the student had loss of control and if I did not take controls I believe it could have led to a fatal accident. [The student is in the] pre-solo phase of training with about 105 hours of dual received. The next day we did a debrief on the flight and when I brought up the events; he interrupted me and said he disagreed with it; when I asked him what he meant by it; he stated that if I wasn't there he would have recovered safely and that I was making him nervous.,,,,Flight Instructor reported that during landing rollout the student lost directional control of the aircraft through misapplication of the rudder pedals and locking up the brakes. The Flight Instructor regained control of the aircraft and safely exited the runway.
1849152,202110,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,,1600,,VMC,10,,Daylight,CLR,,,FBO,Cessna 152,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Climb,None,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Not Flying,Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Instrument; Flight Crew Private; Flight Crew Multiengine,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 20; Flight Crew Total 614; Flight Crew Type 75,,Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Flight Crew,,1849152,,,,,,,,,,,,Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance,,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,General None Reported / Taken,Human Factors,Human Factors,My student and I were turning base to final when my student was cleared for the touch and go and the Tower told us to make right traffic after touch and go. My student read back the landing clearance and did not read back right traffic. I came over the radio and read back the remainder of the call for right traffic to be made. I was talking to my student the whole way down to landing. I was talking a lot to them as they were putting in too much crosswind correction. They were a little behind the aircraft; so I was helping. Upon takeoff we cleaned everything up and took off and incidentally made a mistake and turned left traffic. We did not realize the mistake that had been made until after we were midfield left downwind. Tower did not say anything; nor were we that close to any airplanes (nothing that isn't close for a normal traffic pattern where training is being done). The student and I both should have realized that we needed to turn right traffic after we were clear of the departure end and we were at least 500 ft. off the ground. From now on as an instructor; I will be making taking more precaution to be more aware and to make the correct decisions. I instill in all of my students to ask if you are not sure; do not do something that could potentially put you in a bad situation. I let this moment slip. I will take it and learn from it.,Reporter had no additional information to note.,,,Cessna 152 Flight Instructor reported they made closed traffic in the wrong direction.

1852164,202110,0601-1200,ZZZ.Airport,US,,,,6800,,VMC,,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,,Visual Approach,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Tower ZZZ,Personal,Luscombe (Silvaire) Undifferentiated or Other Model,,1,Part 91,None,Personal,,Climb,None,Class D ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor; Pilot Flying,Flight Crew Commercial; Flight Crew Flight Instructor; Flight Crew Instrument,Flight Crew Last 90 Days 80; Flight Crew Total 530; Flight Crew Type 400,,Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 Other,,1852164,,,,,,,,,,,,Conflict NMAC,Horizontal 200; Vertical 100,,Automation Aircraft TA; Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,My student and I had just departed Runway XXR to do some training in the traffic pattern in ZZZ. We were instructed to extend our departure leg to allow aircraft on the parallel to turn crosswind before us. After that; Aircraft Z turned crosswind. We were given clearance to turn crosswind about another mile beyond them to join left traffic for XXL to start pattern work. Aircraft Y behind me was given instruction to extend upwind and to look for Aircraft X traffic on the crosswind leg - my student and I - and to report them in sight. He reported that he had the Aircraft Z traffic in sight and Tower gave them instructions to turn crosswind north of the Aircraft X traffic. Aircraft Y appeared to have seen the Aircraft Z ahead of us that was already on downwind but had not seen us turning crosswind to downwind. On downwind; I heard the situation play out on the radio and became aware of a potential hazard as we approached the normal crosswind leg. I saw an aircraft on the ADS-B screen on our transponder showing it approaching from our left and climbing with 200 - 100 feet below. I grabbed controls of the aircraft as Tower began advising Aircraft Y of Aircraft X traffic ahead; and told him to descend 200 feet immediately. I saw the aircraft approaching us directly from the left and did a climbing left-hand chandelle to avoid the converging traffic that appeared to still be climbing. I am not certain that they saw us in time to begin a descent; which is why I did not initiate a right-hand turn as stated in Part 91 for right-of-way rules. The aircraft departed the airspace to the west and we continued flying out traffic pattern with no action towards the other aircraft from ATC.,,,,C172 Flight Instructor reported having to execute an evasive maneuver during an NMAC event while on visual approach as the other aircraft misidentified traffic; resulting in a loss of separation.

1854208,202111,1201-1800,ZZZ.Airport,US,320,7,,2200,,Marginal,10,,Daylight,,,Tower ZZZ,FBO,Skyhawk 172/Cutlass 172,,2,Other Part 141,None,Training,,Descent,Visual Approach,Class D ZZZ; Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Military Trainer,,2,Part 91,None,Training,,Final Approach,,Class E ZZZ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Aircraft X,Flight Deck,FBO,Instructor,Flight Crew Flight Instructor,,,Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown,Party1 Flight Crew; Party2 ATC,,1854208,,,,,,,,,,,,ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy,Horizontal 200; Vertical 200,,Person Flight Crew,In-flight,Flight Crew Took Evasive Action,Human Factors,Human Factors,Toward the end of my hour and a half flight block at ZZZ; my student and I were transitioning back to ZZZ from a local airport (ZZZ1) where we conducted practice landings and maneuvers in our designated practice area in which we were ramped out by dispatch to.
